narrate.summary: The paper monitors high-dimensional transmission sensor time series collected during end-of-line testing at Ford. Its method targets unusual patterns in the signals after addressing repeated test cycles, timing differences, and physical relationships between paired measurements. It smooths and aligns the data, uses regression residuals for coupled signals, and reduces the data with kernel principal component analysis. Separate Phase I Hotelling T-squared charts signal an anomaly when a score exceeds its upper control limit, and a weighted score ranks flagged transmissions. In a Phase 90 evaluation, the method detected all confirmed anomalies in two tested subsets, while the first-subset comparison reported better accuracy, recall, and F1 score than the company model.
narrate.key_results: The production case began with 502 transmissions; after exclusions and removal of 85 transmissions with atypical converter outlet pressure behavior, 387 remained for the main analysis. Five phase-specific charts were calibrated to an overall Type I error rate of 0.0027, giving a per-phase significance level of approximately 0.00054. In the first Phase 90 subset, the proposed method reported accuracy 0.625, precision 0.625, recall 1.00, and F1 score 0.769, compared with 0.50, 0.75, 0.30, and 0.429 for the company model; the evaluation used the flagged transmissions and the available warranty and expert labels. In the second subset the reported accuracy was 0.60 and the F1 score was 0.75, and in the third subset the method detected all three confirmed anomalies while flagging 0.0056 of the dataset.

key_equations.name: Hotelling monitoring statistic
key_equations.explanation: The statistic T-squared is the squared Mahalanobis distance of score vector x from the estimated in-control mean vector μ, using the estimated covariance matrix Σ.

key_equations.name: Phase I upper control limit
key_equations.explanation: The upper control limit uses the upper α percentile of the Beta distribution with parameters p divided by 2 and (m minus p minus 1) divided by 2; m is the in-control sample size and p is the score dimension.

narrate.limitations_stated: For the main production dataset, the authors say that insufficient time had passed for warranty information to become available and that no established expert evaluation protocol existed for the studied phases. Expert feedback was available only for transmissions flagged by the method in one evaluation subset, and no expert feedback was available for the third subset.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main case uses a small, single-company production sample, and the paper does not establish performance across other plants, transmission types, or operating periods. The Phase I limits and score-space parameters are estimated from data, but the evaluation does not clearly demonstrate independent validation of those estimates; temporal dependence after alignment and departures from the assumptions behind the Beta-based limit could affect false-alarm rates. The labeled evaluation is based on selected flagged cases and sparse confirmed failures, and the comparison is limited to the company model rather than a broader set of statistical monitoring charts.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to a semi-supervised setting using some reference anomaly data to reduce false positives. They also propose combining the current feature-extraction and monitoring stages into an end-to-end method.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the estimated control limits under autocorrelation, non-normal score distributions, and changes in operating conditions, using independent time-based and cross-site validation. It could also test the full screening process with labels for both flagged and unflagged units, add tools to trace a signal back to contributing sensors and phases after an alarm, and assess the method in a live production deployment.

narrate.summary: The paper presents MODERN, a framework that monitors product images for changes in manufacturing quality and estimates the defective region after a signal. A convolutional neural network estimates the likelihood that each image contains a defect, and an exponentially weighted moving average chart accumulates evidence of an upward shift in that likelihood. The chart signals when its statistic exceeds a control limit calibrated to a target in-control average run length. The framework also includes a transfer procedure for checking whether a pretrained model can be used in a new setting and recalibrating its control limit with a relatively small reference sample. The authors report prompt detection and useful defect localization on benchmark, simulated, and real manufacturing images, with better simulated detection timing than the Markov Field comparison method.
narrate.key_results: On the industrial benchmark, with an in-control average run length of 1,000, the chart’s out-of-control average run length ranged from 20.45 to 21.01 when the change began at observation 21; it signaled exactly at the change point in 94% to 100% of runs across the ten classes. Average defect-region overlap scores across those classes ranged from 0.6036 to 0.8820. In simulated images with Markov Field properties and an in-control average run length of 200, MODERN signaled at observation 21 for both defect types, while the comparison method had average run lengths of 153.75 and 150.58 and signaled at the change point in 1% and 0% of runs, respectively. In the commutator example the chart signaled at the change point, observation 15, with an in-control average run length of 25; in the leather example, both methods warned at observation 22 after the change at observation 21, but the comparison method also produced two false signals before the change.

key_equations.name: Charting statistic
key_equations.explanation: At time t, E_t is the charting statistic, E_{t-1} is its previous value, lambda is the weighting parameter, p-hat_t is the estimated defect probability for the current image, and mu_IC is the mean estimated defect probability for in-control images.

key_equations.name: Signal limit
key_equations.explanation: The chart signals when E_t, its current statistic, exceeds the limit formed from rho, the control-limit multiplier, lambda, the weighting parameter, and sigma_IC, the in-control standard deviation of the estimated defect probabilities.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that manufacturers may have too few defective images to train a network from scratch, and that more defective examples may be needed if the transferred diagnosis model does not locate the faulty region adequately. They do not provide a separate limitations discussion.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real manufacturing demonstrations use very small numbers of images in the commutator case and an ordered monitoring sequence constructed from available examples in the leather case, so they provide limited evidence about performance across operating shifts in sustained production. The paper does not evaluate how serial dependence in successive images or departures from the assumptions behind its applicability t-test affect false-signal rates and control-limit calibration. Its direct method comparison is mainly against the Markov Field approach, and the reported evidence does not establish performance against a broader range of image-monitoring charts.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose randomized controlled experiments with industry partners to evaluate MODERN in real operating settings and to obtain further operational insights. They also suggest applying the framework beyond manufacturing, including food quality, crop surveillance, and environmental image monitoring.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could calibrate the chart for dependent image streams and test robustness when the defect-probability scores do not follow the assumptions used for calibration. Larger prospective production studies could compare more monitoring methods and assess whether regional defect estimates help identify root causes, including defects that are not well represented by an ellipse.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces persistent Laplacian cumulative sum (PL-CUSUM) to monitor multivariate time series for changes in the structure of observations within sliding windows. It embeds each window as a point cloud and extracts persistent Betti features and positive persistent Laplacian spectra. A ridge-whitened projection turns these features into a scalar score, and a cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart adds the score over time and signals when its statistic crosses a calibrated limit. The method is intended to detect changes in high-dimensional, nonlinear processes without specifying a parametric joint distribution for the raw observations. The authors report that the spectral features can detect changes that persistent Betti features miss, and that PL-CUSUM performed strongly in their simulations and real-data examples.
narrate.key_results: In the synthetic tree experiment, persistent Betti features alone had zero detection probability at every tested tilt strength, while the positive-spectrum and full persistent Laplacian features reached detection probabilities from 0.211 at tilt strength 0.20 to 0.955 at 0.80; median pre-change alarm probability ranged from 0.0480 to 0.0497. With the post-change distribution known, the median detection probabilities of PL-CUSUM and the likelihood-ratio benchmark differed by at most 0.0102, and the median correlation between their scores exceeded 0.9999999998. In the oracle simulation, mean detection delay followed a fitted relation with slope 1.4255 and R-squared 0.9983 against log average run length divided by squared ridge-whitened separation; the paper’s theory gives both upper and local minimax lower delay bounds of the same order. For the real-data comparison at target average run length 1,000, PL-CUSUM had success rates from 0.998 to 1.000 and conditional expected delays from 0 to 0.09 across five tasks; no false alarms were observed in four tasks’ 2,000 in-control paths, while the motor background-vibration task had estimated average run length 18,081.6.

key_equations.explanation: S_n is the chart statistic at monitoring step n, S_0 is its starting value, s-hat_n is the estimated scalar score, c-hat is the estimated reference value, eta is the control limit, and T_eta is the first step at which the chart signals.

key_equations.name: Sufficient finite-horizon control limit
key_equations.explanation: Eta is a sufficient control limit, C_dep accounts for dependence, sigma squared bounds score fluctuations, gamma_eff is the separation after estimation error, N is the monitoring horizon, and alpha is the allowed false-alarm probability.

key_equations.name: Oracle detection-delay order
key_equations.explanation: Delay denotes the detection-delay order, A is the required in-control average run length, and gamma_rho is the ridge-whitened separation between states.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their local minimax theory assumes a finite-support exponential-tilting model and does not cover continuous feature values without additional conditions. They also note that the current window features cannot distinguish states that contain the same delay vectors in a different order, and that their model does not cover a transition-law change when the feature marginal distribution remains unchanged.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data evaluation covers one public process dataset and a designed motor-vibration fault scenario, with results based on finite, task-specific samples and selected change points; the very high detection rates therefore do not establish performance across a broad range of operating conditions or gradual changes. The finite-horizon guarantees also rely on concentration assumptions and independent Phase I training windows, while overlapping windows create dependence that can increase the bound; the paper does not report computational runtime or deployment-scale cost for computing the persistent Laplacian features.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the theory to continuous feature values using local moment-generating-function conditions. They also suggest constructing weighted or directed graphs from delay vectors to represent within-window transitions, and using zigzag persistence to track topological change across windows.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the chart prospectively on longer operational streams with gradual changes, multiple changes, and a wider range of fault conditions, while assessing false-alarm behavior over longer horizons. It could also add post-signal diagnosis to identify which channels or geometric features drove an alarm, and measure computational and memory requirements for practical online deployment.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart to monitor the ratio of two normally distributed quality characteristics during a short production run. It uses the ratio of the sample means as the observation and focuses on detecting upward changes in the ratio. The chart accumulates information across inspections and signals when its statistic reaches or exceeds the upper control limit, which is calibrated for the finite inspection horizon. The authors calculate performance using the truncated average run length (TARL) and a Markov-chain approximation. Their main finding is that the chart detects small and moderate upward shifts faster than the compared Shewhart-type chart, with the strongest reported improvement for shifts of 1% to 5%.
narrate.key_results: The study evaluated 200 chart-design configurations and 1,800 shift scenarios, with the in-control TARL generally calibrated close to its target. In the equal-coefficient-of-variation setting with both coefficients equal to 0.2, correlation 0.4, smoothing constant 0.2, horizon 10, and target TARL 10, the out-of-control TARL for a shift factor of 1.05 fell from 8.615 at sample size 1 to 2.713 at sample size 15. Across upward shift factors 1.01, 1.02, and 1.05, the proposed chart reduced TARL by approximately 15% to 40% compared with the Shewhart-type short-run ratio chart in equal-coefficient-of-variation cases with moderate-to-large variation; the charts were essentially equivalent for shifts of at least 1.10. In the beverage-filling illustration, a 5% upward shift beginning at inspection 9 was signaled at inspection 10.

key_equations.name: EWMA chart statistic
key_equations.explanation: W_i is the chart statistic at inspection i, lambda is the smoothing constant, Zhat_i is the ratio of sample means at inspection i, and W_{i-1} is the chart statistic at the previous inspection.

key_equations.name: Signal rule
key_equations.explanation: W_i is the chart statistic at inspection i, and U is the upper control limit; the chart signals when the statistic reaches or exceeds that limit.

key_equations.name: Control-limit calibration
key_equations.explanation: TARL_0(U) is the in-control truncated average run length at upper control limit U, and TARL*_0 is the prescribed target in-control truncated average run length.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors caution that their robustness study covers only the moderate non-normal distributions tested, with matched means, coefficients of variation, and correlations, and with sample size 5. They note that stronger departures from normality and asymmetric tail dependence may require separate treatment, and that the fast distribution approximation may be less accurate for small samples and large coefficients of variation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper does not evaluate how dependence between successive inspection samples would affect the chart’s false-alarm rate or detection performance, even though dependence could change how evidence accumulates in the EWMA statistic. Its performance comparison is limited to one Shewhart-type short-run chart, so it does not establish how the proposed chart compares with other memory-based or adaptive alternatives on the same study grid.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose a two-sided version, adaptive sampling through variable sampling intervals or sample sizes, and an economic-statistical design for the finite horizon. They also propose using direct integration of the exact ratio density for more accurate calibration and extending robustness tests to heavier tails, stronger skewness, and non-Gaussian dependence. They identify a chart that accounts for estimation error in the in-control parameters as an important direction for short-run use.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the chart on real production records and report whether the modeled inspection schedule and shift patterns reflect operational practice. Further work could also develop a systematic post-signal diagnosis procedure to help users identify which of the two measured characteristics drove a change in their ratio.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how measurement error affects two one-sided Synthetic control charts that monitor the ratio of two normally distributed quality variables. The charts use the observed ratio of sample means and combine a Shewhart sub-chart with a conforming-run-length sub-chart. A chart signals only when a ratio observation crosses its one-sided control limit and the associated conforming run length is at or below its limit. The authors calculate zero-state and steady-state run lengths using a Markov chain, under a linear covariate measurement-error model. Their numerical results show that measurement error degrades detection, while taking repeated measurements on each unit provides little improvement.
narrate.key_results: The designs were calibrated to an in-control average run length of 200, and the numerical study considered sample sizes from 1 to 15. Across the examined parameter combinations, increasing sample size from 1 to 15 reduced the expected average run length by roughly a factor of two to three; steady-state values were about 15–20% higher than zero-state values. Increasing precision error worsened detection, while the effect of accuracy error and measurement-error correlation depended on the process correlations. Increasing repeated measurements per unit from 1 to 10 produced no appreciable performance gain. In the battery-recycling illustration, with a sample size of 5 and a downward shift of at most 1% beginning at sample 11, the chart signaled at sample 13.

key_equations.explanation: A signal occurs when the ratio statistic crosses the lower or upper control limit and its conforming run length is no greater than the corresponding limit.

key_equations.name: Zero-state and steady-state run lengths
key_equations.explanation: The zero-state average run length uses initial transient-state probabilities q, the steady-state average run length uses steady-state probabilities ψ, Q is the transient-state transition matrix, I is the identity matrix, and 1 is a column vector of ones.

key_equations.name: Expected average run length

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors caution that their comparison with the Shewhart ratio chart is not entirely on equal terms because the studies use slightly different versions of the measurement-error model and different chart families. They do not state other explicit limitations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The calculations assume normally distributed variables and use an approximate ratio distribution whose accuracy is justified in the paper for relatively small coefficients of variation. The study also treats process and measurement-error parameters as known, explores a selected grid of simulated settings, and offers only an illustrative application rather than validation on operational data; performance with estimated parameters, serial dependence, or non-normal variables is therefore not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose combining the Synthetic ratio chart with variable sampling intervals, variable sample sizes, or run rules to reduce measurement-error effects. They also suggest developing Synthetic charts based on exponentially weighted moving averages or cumulative sums under measurement error, and extending the work to multivariate ratios.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could quantify the effect of estimating the process and measurement-system parameters from limited calibration data, and assess robustness to autocorrelation and non-normal quality variables. It could also validate the chart using real production data and examine procedures for diagnosing the cause and direction of a signal.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors the ratio of two correlated normal quality measurements during a short production run. It proposes an upper one-sided cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart that detects sustained increases in the ratio. The method chooses both the reference value and the decision interval to meet a target in-control truncated average run length (TARL) while reducing the out-of-control TARL at a selected shift. The chart signals when its accumulated statistic reaches or exceeds the decision interval. In the reported comparisons, memory-based charts outperform the Shewhart chart, and the adaptive design can improve detection when correlation increases between the design and monitoring periods.
narrate.key_results: With an in-control target TARL of 30 and a target ratio shift of 1.05, joint optimization reduced out-of-control TARL by 0.69% to 1.36% compared with the fixed-reference design across the reported configurations. For equal coefficients of variation, subgroup size 5, and correlation increasing from 0.4 to 0.8, the adaptive chart’s out-of-control TARL at shift 1.05 was 21.59, compared with 23.22 for fixed-reference CUSUM and 26.46 for the exponentially weighted moving average chart. In the very-low-variability boundary example, the fixed-reference design could not attain the target TARL of 30 and achieved 30.99 to 31, while the adaptive design attained 30 with subgroup sizes 5, 10, and 15. Under contamination, the simulated in-control TARL fell to 28.35 at 5% contamination and 26.67 at 10%; with 100 Phase I subgroups, the relative bias in achieved in-control TARL was about 1%.

key_equations.explanation: Here C_i^+ is the upper cumulative sum at inspection i, C_0^+ is its initial value, Z-hat_i is the sample-mean ratio, k is the reference value, and h is the decision interval.

key_equations.name: Truncated run-length expectation
key_equations.explanation: Here TARL_j is the expected run length truncated at the end of the production run, E_j is expectation in process state j, RL is the run length, I is the number of planned inspections, and state 0 or 1 denotes in-control or out-of-control operation.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the chart is designed for detecting upward shifts and does not cover lower-sided or two-sided monitoring. They also report that contamination can lower the achieved in-control TARL and that estimating parameters from small Phase I samples can produce a biased and variable achieved TARL.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical study mainly uses an in-control ratio of 1, a target shift of 1.05, a horizon with 30 planned inspections, subgroup sizes of 5 or 10, and a limited set of variability and correlation combinations, so results may not generalize to other operating conditions. The outer search relies on empirical unimodality and a finite candidate grid, and the study does not evaluate autocorrelated observations or validate the chart on a real production data set.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose lower-sided and two-sided versions, robust estimators for contamination, and a self-starting design that updates using Phase II data. They also suggest comparison with variable-sampling-interval CUSUM charts and extensions to multivariate ratios, measurement error, and autocorrelation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: The method should be tested on real production data and on broader combinations of run lengths, shift sizes, subgroup sizes, and correlation changes. Further work could also assess procedures for diagnosing the cause of a signal and provide a readily installable software implementation with reproducible examples.

narrate.summary: The paper discusses how statistical monitoring could help assess large language models (LLMs) after deployment. It recommends treating repeated interactions, context, and feedback as a dependent process rather than judging each prompt and response in isolation. A monitored score could summarize properties such as reliability, calibration, safety, or task performance. The chart signals an alarm when a detection statistic based on the monitored scores exceeds a threshold. The paper argues that this sequential perspective connects validity and monitoring, but it does not propose or evaluate a specific chart.
narrate.key_results: This is a discussion paper, not an empirical comparison, and it reports no numerical detection or run-length results. Its main contribution is a framework that connects interaction-level representation, validity under dependence and repeated use, and post-deployment monitoring. The paper proposes monitoring task-specific scores and using sequential alarms to identify changes in system behavior.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors whether a continuously distributed process has developed serial dependence, using short sequences of observations rather than assuming a particular marginal distribution. It converts each sequence of three observations into an ordinal pattern and then forms transcripts between consecutive patterns, also using the associated Kendall distances. Three exponentially weighted moving average charts track changes in transcript probabilities, distance probabilities, or the mean distance. A chart signals when its statistic crosses a simulation-calibrated control limit. Simulations and an example involving chemical-process yields show that the new charts can detect several kinds of dependence and often perform better than earlier ordinal-pattern charts.
narrate.key_results: The authors calibrated the charts to an in-control average run length of 370; the reported values across the tested smoothing settings ranged from 369.6 to 370.5. For an autoregressive process with parameter 0.8 and smoothing parameter 0.05, the Kendall-distance mean chart had an out-of-control average run length of 33.7; with parameter negative 0.8 and the same smoothing value, the Kendall-distance distribution chart had a value of 25.2. For negative autoregressive dependence, the authors found that the lower smoothing setting was important, while the Kendall-distance mean chart performed best overall; for the quadratic moving-average process, the transcript-distribution chart with smoothing parameter 0.05 was strongest among the new charts. In the example of 70 chemical-process yields, the lag-one sample autocorrelation was about negative 0.588, and the Kendall-distance mean chart signaled at observation 23 with smoothing parameter 0.05, compared with observation 24 for the distance-distribution chart and observation 25 for the transcript-distribution chart.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors behavior in a multi-agent system by representing each agent’s query responses over time and summarizing the system’s changing state. It applies a Shewhart-type chart to a scalar statistic of this system-level representation, with control limits that are recalculated from a moving window of recent observations. The chart signals when the statistic falls outside those limits. The authors find that adaptive limits help distinguish natural system drift from anomalies, but they also allow sufficiently gradual adversarial changes to become part of the monitored baseline. Their central conclusion is that adapting to legitimate learning creates a vulnerability to slow adversarial drift.
narrate.key_results: In the simulated environment, agents with static memory fell to about 20% accuracy on changing environmental queries, while agents with dynamic memory maintained substantially higher accuracy. With a reference window of 200 observations, adaptive control tracked natural drift better than fixed limits calibrated on observations 100 through 300. In 100 replications, attacks starting at time 400 and reaching a 0.5 defection probability produced lower alarm-exceedance rates when ramped over 800 rather than 100 iterations; the slow attack was nearly indistinguishable from the no-adversary baseline at a threshold multiplier of 5. The theory establishes that, under its stated assumptions, a sleeper agent can produce any target displacement over a finite sequence of small shifts while making the excess alarm probability approach zero.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Bayesian methods for Phase II statistical process control (SPC) when the practical goal is to know whether a process is acceptable now, not just whether it changed in the past. One method tracks whether a process can move between in-control and out-of-control periods and later recover; the other tracks a changing process parameter against an acceptable region. A signal occurs when the posterior probability of current acceptability falls below a threshold, which the authors calibrate using simulated in-control data. The methods are evaluated with simulations and a held-out multivariate wine-quality illustration built from observations that were not naturally ordered in time. In the principal time-between-failure simulation, the Bayesian method detected changes and recovery sooner on average than the classical comparator, while results depended on the assumed out-of-control behavior and the amount of Phase I information.
narrate.key_results: For the recoverable time-between-failure simulations, the in-control failure rate was 10, out-of-control rates were 40 and 50, and the geometric regime durations had mean 200; the Phase I sample size was 50. The posterior threshold was calibrated to δ = 0.485, targeting one false-signal episode in 200 in-control observations, and achieved 0.992 episodes in calibration. Across 1,000 recoverable sequences, mean detection delays for the two out-of-control episodes were 6.57 and 5.66 observations, and mean recovery delay was 4.56; the classical change-point method had corresponding delays of 7.70, 6.33, and 5.55, with fewer false-signal episodes in this scenario (0.37 versus 0.54). In the Gaussian tracking validation, 5,000 particles gave a root mean squared error of 0.0032 for the posterior acceptable-region probability, with 95% of absolute errors below 0.0070. In the 11-variable wine illustration, mean detection delay was 16.60 observations with a 0.031 miss rate, and mean recovery delay was 1.62 observations; these results came from constructed pseudo-sequences, not a naturally time-ordered production stream.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors six strain measurements from a bridge while accounting for temperature, an environmental and operational variable (EOV). It presents a supervised principal component analysis (PCA) feature-reconstruction method that adjusts for temperature in both the mean and the covariance of the measurements. In tests on the Vahrendorfer Stadtweg bridge, added masses were detectable with the conditional method, while two comparison reconstruction methods did not detect them. The conditional method also reduced false alarms for some of the tested smoothing settings.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used hourly data from six strain sensors and one temperature sensor on one bridge, with added masses of 680 kg, 1,420 kg, and 2,160 kg. For the conditional method, the probability of detection (POD) was 100% at smoothing parameter 0.1, 87.4% at 0.2, 75.73% at 0.3, and 64.08% at 1.0; the unsupervised and partial methods had 0% detection at each of those settings. narrate.summary: The paper develops a probabilistic extension of kernel-based multivariate statistical process control (K-MSPC) for monitoring nonlinear multivariate processes. It estimates kernel parameters deterministically, then uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to represent uncertainty in those parameters and propagates the samples through kernel principal component analysis (K-PCA). The resulting Hotelling’s T-squared (T²) and squared prediction error (SPE) charts show monitoring values alongside uncertainty bands, while contribution plots show uncertainty in variable attribution. The charts signal when monitoring statistics exceed their control limits; in the examples, the bands are narrow during normal operation and widen after faults begin. On the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, posterior-based monitoring often improves detection for the squared exponential kernel, while the automatic relevance determination kernel has narrower uncertainty and similar deterministic and probabilistic performance.
narrate.key_results: Across 21 TEP faults, the mean composite indicator for the squared exponential kernel increased from 0.71 with deterministic prior-mean charts to 0.79 with posterior-mean charts. Reported examples include increases from 0.82 to 0.99 for fault F01, from 0.53 to 0.92 for F14, and from 0.50 to 0.81 for F21. For the automatic relevance determination kernel, the mean composite indicator was 0.79 for both deterministic and posterior-mean charts. In unsupervised calibration, methods M1, M2, M3, M6, M8, M9, and M10 had mean scores from 0.83 to 0.84 across the faults; the M8 method used for probabilistic monitoring scored 0.84. The paper reports no run-length results; for the squared exponential kernel, the adaptive Metropolis sampler with delayed rejection had effective sample sizes of approximately 305 to 486 across parameters.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for monitoring changes in covariance among multiple functional profiles, such as temperature curves from several sensors. It uses multichannel functional principal component analysis (MFPCA) and a functional graphical model to represent conditional relationships between profiles. The chart accumulates covariance information over time and combines likelihood-ratio tests for different assumed numbers of changed relationships using nonparametric combination (NPC). It signals when the combined statistic exceeds a control limit calibrated to a target average run length (ARL), and its diagnostic procedure identifies likely changed relationships and estimates a change point. Simulations and a roasting-machine case study show that the proposed multichannel profile covariance (MPC) chart detects the studied changes more effectively than the two comparison methods.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, the in-control target average run length was 100; the authors report that all methods had in-control run lengths at least as large as this target. The simulations used three profile counts (10, 20, and 30), four shift patterns, severity levels from 0 to 4, and 1, 3, 5, or 10 shifted elements; the MPC chart generally had lower out-of-control run lengths than the hierarchical graphical model and the method of Ren and colleagues, especially for sparse shifts. In the roasting-process example, 200 out-of-control sequences were monitored, and the estimated average run lengths were 12.340 for MPC, 34.585 for the hierarchical graphical model, and 17.710 for the Ren method. For an illustrative sequence, the chart signaled at observation 65, estimated a change point at observation 57, and identified relationships involving sensor 8 and sensors 7 and 9 using a false discovery rate of 0.01. The paper reports that the calculations and plots used the R language and that supplementary materials include R code for reproducing the case-study results.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to nonparametric settings, incorporating temporal dependence between successive multichannel profiles, and developing methods that distinguish natural nonstationarity from anomalous covariance shifts.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the chart prospectively on independent production data and across multiple manufacturing processes, including assessment of the effects of Phase I sample size and parameter-estimation uncertainty on false alarms and detection. narrate.summary: The paper develops probability bounds for the largest absolute cumulative deviation in negative binomial (NB) count data. For independent counts, it gives a variance-based threshold using the mean and overdispersion of each count. For dependent counts, it studies a Poisson model with a shared Gamma mixing variable and derives both a polynomial bound and an exponential bound. The monitoring signal is raised when the largest absolute centered partial sum exceeds the chosen threshold. The authors report that shared mixing can substantially increase maximum deviations, and illustrate the method using a COVID-19 surveillance example. The method is based on maximal partial sums, not a conventional cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart.
narrate.key_results: In a moment-matched simulation with 20 counts and 2,000 replications, the dependent case had a mean maximum deviation of 42.22 and a 95th percentile of 101.43, compared with 17.74 and 33.16 for the independent case. The corresponding theoretical thresholds were 476.52 for the dependent case and 72.49 for the independent case. In the surveillance example, five regions were monitored over 12 weeks; the independent-case 95% threshold was about 6,370 cases, while the simulated 95th percentile was about 3,018 cases, giving 47% bound efficiency. The authors also state that their dependent-case Bernstein-type bound has exponential rather than polynomial decay.

narrate.summary: The paper presents VSCOUT, a method for retrospective monitoring of high-dimensional process data that may be contaminated, non-Gaussian, or nonlinear. It first learns a compact latent representation, then uses an ensemble of outlier detectors and changepoint analysis to find isolated anomalies and sustained changes. After provisionally removing flagged observations, it retrains the model on the retained in-control data and evaluates observations using changepoint, ensemble, latent-distance, and reconstruction-error indicators. An observation is labelled out of control when at least two of these four indicators signal. Simulations and benchmark data show that the method can identify anomalies while generally keeping false alarms controlled, although performance varies across data types.
narrate.key_results: In outlier-free simulations, the reported average false positive rate was 0.0418, compared with the nominal level of 0.05. Across simulated transient shifts, VSCOUT had average recall of 0.7455 and false positive rate of 0.0311; for sustained shifts, the corresponding values were 0.7543 and 0.0306. For sustained shifts at high contamination levels of 10%, 15%, and 20%, its average F1 score was 0.7483, the second-highest among the methods in the comparison. Across benchmark anomaly-detection datasets, average recall was 0.4545 and average AUROC was 0.7924; on the semiconductor sensor dataset in Phase I, recall was 0.1519 and false positive rate was 0.1050.

key_equations.name: Final two-of-four decision rule
key_equations.explanation: The predicted out-of-control label for observation i is y-hat_i; the four binary indicators are c_i for changepoint, e_i for ensemble, u_i for Hotelling-statistic exceedance, and q_i for reconstruction-error exceedance; the indicator function returns one when at least two flags are present.

key_equations.name: Approximate global false-alarm probability
key_equations.explanation: Alpha_global is the approximate overall in-control false-alarm probability; alpha_cp, alpha_ens, alpha_T-squared, and alpha_rec are the component false-alarm probabilities for changepoint, ensemble, Hotelling statistic, and reconstruction error; the approximation replaces joint probabilities by products of marginal probabilities.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that performance degrades on datasets such as optdigits, where anomalies are weakly separated and do not align well with latent reconstruction structure. They also describe the semiconductor dataset as difficult for unsupervised detection, with modest overall separation. They note that the estimated latent covariance can be ill-conditioned when the retained in-control sample is extremely small, and suggest that a regularized covariance estimator may be used in that case.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The changepoint procedure treats the earliest detected changepoint as the onset of a shift and flags every later observation, so it may not represent multiple changes, recoveries, or nonpersistent regimes well. Simulations use samples of 500 observations, dimensions of 150 or 250, and global mean shifts applied across all features; this leaves other temporal dependence patterns and localized or gradual process changes less tested. The global false-alarm calculation relies on an approximate independence assumption even though the paper notes that its indicators can be correlated, and empirical calibration may therefore be important in applications.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending VSCOUT to fully online Phase II monitoring, incorporating temporal or attention-based latent structures, and developing formal uncertainty quantification for latent relevance and anomaly decisions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method under serial correlation, gradual drift, multiple operating regimes, and shifts affecting only selected variables, then validate the control limits on a wider range of real industrial processes. It would also be useful to study how to diagnose the cause of a signal and to assess how sensitive the results are to detector selection, changepoint penalties, and estimated in-control parameters.

narrate.summary: The paper develops statistical process control charts that monitor a process by calculating a p-value at each time point. A basic chart signals when the p-value falls at or below a chosen threshold, and its false-alarm guarantees hold even when dependence over time is unrestricted, provided the p-values are valid. The authors also construct smoothed charts by combining p-values, and a multivariate procedure that identifies affected coordinates and directions of change. Their main finding is that these methods give distribution-free guarantees for alarm timing and false localization, although some smoothed charts can be conservative.
narrate.key_results: With valid p-values and no assumptions about dependence over time, the authors prove a lower bound of (1 + 1/α)/2 for the average run length and (1 + k/α)/2 for the expected time to the k-th alarm; under conditional validity, the bounds improve to 1/α and k/α. In simulations of Kolmogorov–Smirnov p-value charts, using 100 repetitions per setting, the observed average run lengths were 6.51 to 32.94 times the theoretical lower bound across reference sample sizes of 20, 50, and 100, alarm levels of 0.01 and 0.05, and first- or fifth-alarm measurements. For the tested smoothed charts, the reported ratios to the lower bound ranged as high as about 3,500, illustrating potentially substantial conservatism. In the multivariate examples, one-time family-wise error estimates from 10,000 simulations remained below the selected 0.01 or 0.05 level in the reported normal and Cauchy settings.

key_equations.explanation: R is the time of the first alarm, t is the time point, P_t is the p-value at that time, and α is the alarm threshold.

key_equations.name: Run-length lower bounds
key_equations.explanation: ARL is the expected time to the first alarm, k-ARL is the expected time to the k-th alarm, k is the alarm count, and α is the chosen threshold; the first pair needs only valid p-values, while the sharper pair requires conditional validity.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the distribution-free run-length bounds can be conservative when temporal dependence is unrestricted. Their simulations examine only a limited number of smoothing-parameter combinations, and some smoothed charts show very large in-control run lengths.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The guarantees depend on the input tests producing valid p-values, but in practical applications estimated baselines and nuisance parameters can make validity difficult to establish, especially when reference data are reused. The evaluation is simulation-based and uses selected synthetic distributions and alternatives rather than real production data; comparisons with established chart designs are limited, so practical performance across operating conditions remains uncertain.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing principled ways to select the smoothing parameters to balance detection and in-control conservatism, and studying alternative p-value combination functions. They also propose using dependence among coordinates to improve localization power while preserving family-wise error control.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the methods on real manufacturing or service-process data and study how estimation of the reference distribution affects the guarantees. It would also be useful to develop post-signal diagnostic procedures and accessible software that supports parameter selection, validation of input p-values, and comparison with standard charts.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for monitoring changes in the distributions of damage-sensitive features derived from structural health monitoring data. It estimates a probability density function for each data subgroup, then uses warping functions to represent both shifts and more complex changes in distribution shape. Functional principal component analysis produces monitoring features, and rank-based charts monitor changes in those features. A signal occurs when the chart’s maximum absolute weighted statistic crosses its control limit; the method also estimates when the change began. Simulations and a bridge case study show detection of complex changes and resistance to isolated outliers.
narrate.key_results: In 100 simulated sequences per setting, with an in-control average run length of 500, the method’s detection probability in the 130-point scenario was 0.60 at shift parameter 0.10 and 0.94 at 0.15; the corresponding probabilities for the PDF-based chart and the Bayes change-point method were 0.02 and 0.04 at 0.10. In the 200-point scenario, the proposed method reached 0.99 at shift parameter 0.10, compared with 0.16 and 0.10 for those two alternatives. In an outlier simulation with four anomalous distributions before the true change at index 200, the proposed method estimated the change at 200, while direct charting produced earlier false alarms. For four cable pairs, manually identified change points were 53, 61, 101, and 119; the method’s estimates were 53 or 52, 61, 101, and 118, respectively.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a cumulative standardized binomial exponentially weighted moving average (CSB-EWMA) chart for monitoring binary outcomes from parallel streams. Each observation is recoded as whether it exceeds a known in-control median, and counts are accumulated across streams and time. The method derives the exact, time-varying mean and variance of its exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) statistic, rather than relying on a steady-state approximation from the start. The chart signals when its statistic crosses an upper or lower control limit that changes over time according to the derived variance. Simulations show that the derived moments closely match empirical moments under the tested in-control setting.
narrate.key_results: With 10,000 Monte Carlo replications, 10 independent streams, an in-control proportion of 0.5, and a smoothing parameter of 0.2, the simulated and theoretical variances were 0.6385 and 0.6369 at time 10, and 0.9996 and 0.9978 at time 1000. The paper reports that variance relative bias stayed below 2% at the selected times and that theoretical variance reached 99% of its asymptotic value by time 227. The theoretical mean was zero; the reported simulated means at times 10, 50, 100, 500, and 1000 were -5.54×10⁻³, -5.23×10⁻³, -1.95×10⁻³, -6.06×10⁻⁴, and -3.09×10⁻³. The paper evaluates moment accuracy, not run length or detection performance for shifts.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes combining Statistical Process Control (SPC) with Conformal Prediction (CP) to monitor individual quality measurements and high-dimensional process snapshots. For individual measurements, it compares each observation’s nonconformity score with a threshold estimated from stable reference data; for multivariate monitoring, it converts an anomaly score into a conformal p-value. The charts signal when a score exceeds its threshold or when a p-value falls below the selected significance level, and they also propose using widening prediction intervals as an uncertainty warning. The paper’s plotted examples suggest that the conformal chart flags more observations after simulated mean shifts than a standard Shewhart chart, including for normal and exponential data.
narrate.key_results: The paper shows illustrative simulated mean shifts for normal and exponential data and states that the conformal-enhanced chart is more sensitive to the shifts than the standard Shewhart chart. It reports no shift magnitudes, detection times, false alarm measurements, or run-length results, so the size of the claimed improvement cannot be quantified from the paper. For the individual-observation chart, it gives alpha = 0.0027 as the setting corresponding to the approximately 99.73% coverage of traditional three-standard-deviation limits. For the multivariate p-value chart, it gives example significance levels of 0.05 and 0.01, but does not report quantitative comparative results for that method.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a way to monitor multiple lines when only one line can be sampled at each step. Responses are binary, and the method uses the accumulated likelihood ratio information to favor sampling the line that appears more likely to have changed, while retaining a minimum sampling probability for exploration. For each line, the chart signals when its statistic crosses either the lower or upper control bound. The authors calculate false alarm rates and detection power using exact distributions and compare the method with equal random allocation. In their numerical studies, adaptive sampling generally sends more units to the changed line and gives higher detection power for sample sizes of 20 or more.
narrate.key_results: For two lines with in-control success probability 0.05 and projected out-of-control probability 0.1, at sample size 20 the adaptive method had power 0.17570 for an actual changed-line probability of 0.2, compared with 0.12178 for equal allocation; at an actual probability of 0.3, power was 0.47205 compared with 0.35106. In the same setting at sample size 20, the reported single-line false alarm rates were 0.00182 for adaptive sampling and 0.00103 for equal allocation. At the actual changed-line probability of 0.2, the adaptive method allocated an average proportion of 0.602 of units to the changed line. Across the studied settings, the authors report that the advantage in power generally grows with sample size and with the difference between in-control and out-of-control probabilities.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes Phase I, distribution-free charts for checking historical individual observations for a change in location. Each observation is converted to a zero-or-one label using a threshold, and the method evaluates either the number of success runs or the largest count of successes in a fixed-length window. Exact conditional distributions, calculated given the total number of successes, provide the chart limits without requiring a specified underlying distribution. The run chart signals on an unusually small number of success runs, while the scan chart signals on an unusually large window count; randomization can be used when discreteness prevents the requested false-signal probability from being attained exactly. Simulations indicate that the charts maintain the intended in-control signal probability and have useful detection performance, especially for heavy-tailed data, while results are weaker for skewed data.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used nominal in-control signal probability 0.005, sample sizes 50 and 100, and normal, exponential, and t distributions with 3 degrees of freedom; the tested shift sizes ranged from 0 to 3, with change points at the locations specified for the three scenarios. Across the reported chart and distribution settings, simulated in-control signal probabilities ranged from 0.0039 to 0.0059. Compared with the Mann–Whitney, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, and empirical likelihood ratio charts, the proposed charts were reported as satisfactory for normal data and consistently better for the heavy-tailed t distribution, while the comparison charts performed better for exponential data. In the piston-ring example, both proposed chart types identified a potential instability near the end of the 40 sample means: the run statistic was 4 with conditional p-value 0.0253, and the scan statistics were 5 and 7 for window lengths 6 and 10, with reported conditional p-values 0.0123 and 0.0525.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal limitations section. narrate.limitations_unstated: The performance study covers independent observations, three distribution families, sample sizes 50 and 100, and step changes in location; it does not establish behavior under autocorrelation, gradual changes, or other process dynamics. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose applying the framework to other run and pattern statistics, including statistics suited to detecting variance changes. They also note that the one-sided method can be extended to use lower and upper limits to detect shifts in either direction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the charts under autocorrelation, non-step changes, ties, and wider ranges of distribution shapes and sample sizes, and could test threshold-selection strategies with independent reference samples. A useful next step would be broader validation on operational process data and practical guidance or software for interpreting and investigating signals.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors the geometric accuracy of manufactured parts using unstructured, variable-size point cloud data without aligning the scans or reconstructing meshes. It proposes two ways to extract shape features: one based on the Robust Laplacian and another based on geodesic distances. A chart standardizes these features against an in-control reference sample, applies hard thresholding, and raises an alarm when the resulting statistic exceeds a control limit estimated from reference data. The method is intended to detect changes in the feature means, including changes affecting only a few features. Simulations and a manufactured-part case study show that both methods detect global and local defects, with the preferred method depending on defect size and reference noise.
narrate.key_results: In the Stanford Bunny simulations, all methods attained an in-control ARL target of 20; the reported values ranged from 20.30 to 20.74. For global roughness at a defect-to-baseline noise ratio of 1.25, RFM-RL had an average run length of 2.73 and RFM-HM had 4.42, compared with 11.63 for the Graph Laplacian benchmark. For local roughness affecting 2.5% of points at a ratio of 3, RFM-HM had an average run length of 3.35 (standard deviation 0.39), while RFM-RL had 9.15 (1.71); the authors also report that RFM-RL is more sensitive to extremely localized defects and higher in-control noise in their aortic-valve study. In the egg-shell case study, the first 10 parts were in control and the next 10 had a missing strut; both methods correctly identified all 10 defective parts.

key_equations.name: Threshold and chart statistic
key_equations.explanation: The threshold c is determined by the number of features k and a_k; the statistic T at observation t sums squared standardized feature values z for feature j that exceed c in absolute value, with the indicator equal to one when its condition holds and zero otherwise.

key_equations.name: Control limit and alarm rule
key_equations.explanation: The control limit h is the empirical quantile Q at probability one minus alpha of statistics T from tuning observations indexed by the set T; the chart signals when a statistic exceeds h.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the procedures require high-density point clouds, although their simulations use point clouds of tens of thousands of points. They also report that higher in-control noise can mask defects, and that using all pairwise geodesic distances can mask very small-scale defects and reduce detection performance.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence relies mainly on generated isotropic Gaussian noise and a small number of shapes, while the manufactured-part case study examines one type of missing-material defect. The paper does not establish performance under temporally dependent observations or the broader measurement and process variation expected in production; estimated reference parameters and control limits may also perform differently when fewer representative in-control parts are available.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose post-signal diagnostics to locate defects and estimate their spatial spread. They also suggest monitoring shape together with point-wise attributes such as surface texture.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the charts on longer production sequences from multiple manufacturing settings, including realistic scan variability and changing point density. It could also test robustness to non-Gaussian noise and temporal dependence, and assess how reference-sample size affects the accuracy of estimated control limits.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a method for monitoring regression models when labels are costly and concept drift may occur only in part of the input space. PASS allocates a limited labeling budget between sampling near locations with large historical residuals and exploring regions that have not been sampled recently. It monitors newly observed prediction residuals with one-sided exponentially weighted moving average charts, using either the largest absolute residuals or residual variance. A signal occurs when a chart exceeds its calibrated upper control limit. In simulations and a UK electricity-market case study, adaptive sampling detected localized changes with fewer labels than random sampling and, in the case study, performed similarly to monitoring all available observations.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, control limits were calibrated to an in-control average run length of 200, and each setting was evaluated over 100 replications. For abrupt drift affecting 1% of the input domain, with shift magnitudes from 1 to 3 times the noise standard deviation, PASS reduced the average out-of-control run length by 38.62% relative to random sampling. A hybrid that used PASS sampling with the score-vector monitor reduced average run length by 50.38% relative to the nonadaptive score-vector method. Incremental drift was harder to detect than abrupt drift at the same affected-area ratio and shift magnitude. In the electricity-market example, PASS monitored 8 of 48 daily half-hour periods and produced results described as remarkably consistent with full sampling; random sampling missed the earlier March 9 signal and detected only the later August shift.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adaptive tuning of the exploration and exploitation balance, theoretical analysis of detection delays and false-alarm rates, extensions to multivariate targets, and online retraining schemes.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on real processes with independently verified drift times and locations, and examine performance under serial dependence, non-normal residuals, and different forms of localized change. narrate.summary: This review explains how functional data analysis can be used to monitor quality characteristics recorded as profiles. Its reference framework smooths discrete measurements, reduces their dimension using multivariate functional principal component analysis, and monitors both variation captured by the retained components and reconstruction error. A signal occurs when either chart statistic exceeds its control limit, which is estimated from a reference sample assumed to represent stable operation. The review also surveys methods for covariate adjustment, outlier resistance, monitoring partially observed profiles in real time, and adapting monitoring to possible changes. A ship-voyage example illustrates the framework, and the review describes software implementation and identifies open research challenges.
narrate.key_results: The review’s ship example used 144 voyages for the reference data: 104 for model training and 40 for tuning, followed by 50 voyages in Phase II. The control limits were estimated from empirical quantiles of statistics on the tuning data. The charts flagged multiple voyages as potential anomalies; the discussion identifies observation 70 as anomalous on both charts, with contributions from all monitored variables, and describes abnormal transverse wind as a contributor to an anomaly at observation 43. The paper reports no run-length or detection-delay comparisons, since it is a review rather than a comparative performance study.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify unresolved challenges in scaling methods to high-frequency, high-dimensional streams; separating phase and amplitude variation; adapting to evolving processes and small reference samples; and handling partially observed data. They also note that robust methods and diagnostic tools are limited, and that publicly available benchmark data and production-ready software remain scarce.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The review presents one operational example and does not report a systematic evaluation across multiple real processes or a common numerical comparison of the surveyed methods. The reference framework also depends on a representative stable reference sample and empirical calibration, so its practical performance when that sample is small or imperfect is not established by the example.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose research on scalable methods for heterogeneous data streams, automatic separation of phase and amplitude, online adaptation of model parameters, and monitoring with missing or partially observed profiles. They also call for stronger outlier robustness, better root-cause and change-duration diagnosis, optimized industrial software, and more public benchmark datasets.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a shared evaluation using diverse operational data and consistent measures of false alarms and detection delay, including settings with serial dependence and non-normal observations. Further work could also quantify how uncertainty in smoothing, component selection, and empirical control-limit estimation affects alarms, and provide practical guidance for diagnosing signals.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for monitoring the topology of lattice-like parts made by additive manufacturing, using point-cloud or mesh measurements. It computes persistent homology features that describe connected components and loops, then compares each new part with an in-control reference sample using distances between persistence diagrams. The chart signals when the reference-group statistic is unusually small relative to a permutation null distribution formed using the new part. The authors evaluate the method with simulated parts and defects, and compare it with a spectral geometry-monitoring method. Their main finding is that loop-based monitoring detects many simulated defects rapidly, although the spectral method performs better for some small collapse defects and under some noise conditions.
narrate.key_results: With a reference sample of 200 parts and a significance level of 0.05, single-feature in-control average run lengths for the simulated cube and egg cases were generally near the nominal value of 20; the authors recommend at least 200 reference parts. For the egg collapse defect, at a change of one-fifth of the coordinate-noise standard deviation, the combined chart had an average run length of 8.668 parts; for the missing-strut defect at noise level 0.005, the loop chart’s average run length was 15.356 parts and the combined chart’s was 9.385. In the comparison without skeletonization, at the smallest reported collapse change the combined topological chart had an average run length of 3.973, versus 3.414 for the spectral method; for the missing-strut defect at noise level 0.005, the respective values were 1.783 and 2.957.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors whether high-dimensional online process signals retain the learned relationship with corresponding offline product quality data. narrate.key_results: In simulation, the method was comparable to the tested control-chart methods at low noise and had lower Type-II error and higher F1 score as process-signal noise increased; the tested noise standard deviations ranged from 1 to 2. With thresholds adjusted to target a 10% false positive rate, it reported a 10.0% false positive rate, a 14.0% false negative rate, and an F1 score of 87.76%. Under the validation-selected threshold, the comparison methods had false positive rates of 63.5% and 74.0%; under the adjusted threshold, their false negative rates were 83.5% and 77.5%. narrate.summary: The paper proposes charts for monitoring count data with excess zeros and overdispersion using the zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model. The paper reports that EWMA generally performed better, while also noting exceptions for some large shifts and parameter combinations. narrate.summary: The paper monitors bivariate time-between-events data whose two component event times may arrive asynchronously. It transforms each arriving event time using the assumed in-control distribution, producing a sequence intended to be independent exponential observations when the process is in control. An adaptive cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart updates after each arrival, estimates possible shifts in the transformed rates, and combines eight directional charts into a common-scale statistic. The chart signals when that statistic exceeds a calibrated threshold. Simulations and an escalator-maintenance example show earlier detection than the existing real-time Shewhart chart in many settings, especially for sustained changes.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, the target in-control average time to signal (ATS) was 200, and the adaptive chart generally had lower ATS than the Shewhart chart across three bivariate distribution families and four in-control scenarios. For the independent Marshall–Olkin bivariate exponential scenario with baseline means (5, 5), a shift to (5, 2.5) gave ATS values of 60.8 for the adaptive chart and 171.4 for the Shewhart chart; a shift to (1, 1) gave 5.4 and 16, respectively. The advantage was not universal: under the independent Marshall–Olkin bivariate Weibull scenario, the shift from (5, 5) to (10, 10) gave ATS values of 23.4 for the adaptive chart and 22.8 for the Shewhart chart. In the escalator data example, with a target in-control average run length (ARL) of 50, the adaptive chart signaled at the 9th Phase II observation, compared with the Shewhart chart at the 92nd; the authors also report that the adaptive statistic exceeded 5.5 by the 16th observation, a level they say could signal under a more conservative setting near an ARL of 3000.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors changes in the conditional relationship between predictors and a response using score vectors from a fitted predictive model. It uses the multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) chart proposed in earlier work, but develops a nested bootstrap method to set its control limits using the full training sample. The method corrects for excess variability in bootstrap statistics caused by the finite out-of-bag sample. At each monitoring time, the chart signals when its quadratic score statistic exceeds the corresponding time-specific control limit. In simulated examples, the bootstrap limits kept pointwise false-alarm rates close to their targets and allowed the entire initial sample to be used to fit the model.
narrate.key_results: In the linear-mixture example, with 2,000 training observations and a target pointwise false-alarm rate of 0.001, the bootstrap method kept the empirical rate close to 0.001 across 50 replicates, while the earlier two-sample method's rate exceeded 0.06. For one simulated stream, the change began at observation 201 and the chart signaled at observation 258. In the nonlinear oscillator example, across 8,000 Monte Carlo replicates, the pointwise false-alarm rate before the change at observation 200 remained close to 0.001 for noise standard deviations of 0.03 and 0.20; detection probability increased after the change, with a longer average delay at higher noise. narrate.summary: The paper presents a two-part method for adapting data-based process models as operating conditions change. Its monitoring component charts the multivariate distances of model errors and process inputs from reference data. If a batch of errors is no longer consistent with the reference, input distances are checked to determine whether the process is in a new operating condition or whether a previously represented condition has changed internally. A signal for a new condition prompts offline training and addition of a model, while an online Gaussian process corrects residual error between these updates. In a simulated district heating system, the combined method achieved a fitting index of 92.9%, better than the comparison methods reported.
narrate.key_results: In the district heating system simulation, the error chart used the 99.73rd percentile of reference distances as its upper control limit, and the monitoring procedure detected the test condition with thermal demands of 150–350 kW as outside the original training condition of 100–300 kW. On the two-day comparison, the weighted ensemble had a fitting index of 69.5%, compared with 42.1% for one model trained on both datasets and 54.1% for the arithmetic-average ensemble. Adding online correction raised the fitting index to 92.9%, versus 67.8% for the sliding-window Gaussian process and 60.5% for the Gaussian process retaining all samples. Average evaluation times per iteration were 0.829 seconds for the combined method, 0.604 seconds for the ensemble, and 3.451 seconds for the all-samples Gaussian process; the study reports fitting and simulation results, not run-length results.

Its methods look for worsening patterns, especially shorter intervals between events and larger event amplitudes, using an upper-sided EWMA chart and nonparametric change-point charts. narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for structural health monitoring (SHM) that tracks daily profiles of bridge vibration measurements while accounting for temperature-related variation. It models each profile using functional data analysis (FDA), estimates a structural component of the remaining error with functional principal component analysis (FPCA), and monitors the resulting scores with a multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) chart. The chart signals when a distance statistic for the smoothed scores exceeds a calibrated threshold. In data from the KW51 railway bridge, the charts signaled at the beginning of the retrofitting period, but also produced false alarms. The method is illustrated on three natural-frequency modes from one bridge.
narrate.key_results: For the KW51 bridge, the Phase I reference period comprised the first 200 days, but only 145 to 148 profiles were usable for individual models; missing data reached 47.5%. The three modeled modes required four, three, and five functional principal components, respectively, to capture 99% of the structural error variation, giving 12 scores in total. Both chart configurations were calibrated to an in-control average run length (ARL) of 370.4: the threshold was 30.09 for lambda equal to 1 and 29.64 for lambda equal to 0.3. Both charts signaled at the start of retrofitting; the paper reports 12 false alarms for lambda equal to 0.3 and four for lambda equal to 1, with false alarms associated by the authors with cold temperatures near the edge of the fitted temperature range.

narrate.summary: The paper presents an online method for monitoring profiles whose values vary both because of random function coefficients and measurement error. It uses the dependence among locations within a profile to identify changes in means or correlation patterns. For each profile, it calculates conditional probability values at each monitor and combines them using either the minimum or the geometric mean. The chart signals when the chosen combined value falls below a calibrated threshold. Simulations and a glass-transmittance example show that the method can detect changes that a principal-component-based chart may miss, while its false alarm behavior can depend on the aggregation rule and the available reference data.
narrate.key_results: The authors derive that a control limit at the kth reference order statistic gives an in-control average run length (ARL0) of m divided by k minus 1, and show that the run length approaches a geometric distribution as the reference sample grows. In simulations using 10 monitors, 1,000 in-control reference profiles, and a target ARL0 of 1,000, the proposed charts performed comparably to the Hotelling chart for global shifts; the minimum aggregation was weaker for shifts of 0.1 and 0.2, while the geometric mean used information across monitors. For the broken-monitor change, which altered covariance without a mean shift, the minimum rule detected changes faster than the Hotelling chart, while the principal-component chart did not detect them effectively; in the trajectory-switch study, Hotelling detection was slightly faster and the principal-component chart was considerably slower. In the glass example, the data included 192 panels measured at 25 inspection locations and 35 wavelengths; out-of-control profiles were generally detected quickly, but false alarm rates were high for the minimum rule and lower for the geometric-mean rule, especially after increasing the in-control reference set with an adjacent wavelength.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the method assumes a sufficiently large historical data set to learn the in-control process. The number of parameters to estimate increases with the number of monitor sites, and the Gaussianity assumption may be too strong for some applications.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method estimates the mean and covariance from reference profiles, but the paper does not study in detail how errors in those estimates affect detection or false alarm rates when the reference sample is small; the glass example illustrates that false alarm rates can be high with limited reference data. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method beyond Gaussian data using graphical models, including localized dependence structures and regularity assumptions that could reduce the burden of learning from limited historical data. narrate.summary: The paper monitors whether the feature distribution in an unlabeled detection window differs from a labeled reference window, using the training data as a shared baseline. Its batched distance (BD) method calculates a chosen distribution distance for paired training-reference batches and training-detection batches. It applies a paired, two-sided t-test to the differences between those distances and signals drift when the p-value falls below the chosen significance level. In simulations, batched testing generally had better detection performance than permutation testing under a matched computational budget, with results depending on the distance measure and type of shift. The paper also tests combining detector outputs using information from earlier labeled drift assessments, and reports that a multilayer perceptron using p-values achieved the highest reported accuracy in that setting.
narrate.key_results: In the first simulation study, the significance level was 0.05, there were 100 simulation repetitions, and the feature dimension was 100; the authors set computation budgets to about 10^8 iterations for the method comparisons. For a mean shift of 0.04 in all features, the BD method with maximum mean discrepancy had a false-negative rate (FNR) of 0.01 and a false-positive rate (FPR) of 0.03; the univariate Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests with Bonferroni correction had an FNR of 0. For a variance multiplier of 1.05, BD with earth mover’s distance and with Kullback–Leibler divergence each had an FNR of 0; for an off-diagonal covariance shift of 0.07, BD with Kullback–Leibler divergence had an FNR of 0, while BD with maximum mean discrepancy had an FNR of 0.03. In the prior-detection study, the multilayer perceptron using p-values had the highest reported accuracy, 71.4%, but its no-drift FPR was 0.09; the authors report that classifier thresholds were chosen to target an FPR around 0.05.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a statistical monitoring approach for national estimates of SARS-CoV-2 prevalence based on wastewater samples from treatment plants across Austria. It converts virus concentration and wastewater inflow into estimated numbers of fictitious excretors, then combines regional measurements into national time series. The authors test Shewhart, cumulative sum, and Bayesian predictive charts for detecting increases in the monitored estimate. The cumulative sum and Shewhart charts signal when their statistics cross a decision threshold, while the predictive chart signals when a new observation falls outside its predictive interval. The paper finds that sampling twice weekly at 24 sites can preserve the national curve reasonably well, and presents monitoring results as a proof of concept rather than a validated operational alert system.
narrate.key_results: The authors report that the best reduced sampling scenario for the first aggregation method uses 24 treatment plants sampled twice per week; for the second method, the best scenario uses all 48 plants sampled once per week. They conclude that a shared recommendation is to keep the twice-weekly frequency while reducing the sites from 48 to 24. With the cumulative sum chart, the reported in-control average run length is 564; the out-of-control average run lengths are 4.76 for a shift from 45 to 55, 2.8 for a shift from 120 to 150, and 19.89 for a shift from 43 to 47. A further shift from 100 to 150 is detected with an out-of-control average run length of 1.18, and the Bayesian predictive chart correctly flags the July 24, 2023 observation using the preceding two observations for training.
