narrate.summary: The paper monitors multivariate functional quality data, where each item is represented by several profiles, and addresses both whole-observation and individual-profile outliers in the reference sample. Its proposed robust multivariate functional control chart (RoMFCC) filters suspected cellwise outliers, imputes the resulting missing profiles, and uses robust functional principal components to model the data. In Phase II, it monitors changes in the retained component space and in the residual space using Hotelling's T-squared and squared prediction error statistics. It signals when either statistic exceeds its control limit. Simulations and a resistance spot-welding case study find that the method detects mean shifts more effectively than the competing charts considered, including when the reference sample contains outliers.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation study, the authors used 50 runs per setting, with 4,000 observations in each Phase I and Phase II sample; the main contaminated settings used a 0.05 contamination probability, with additional results at 0.1. The study evaluated mean-shift detection at severity levels 1 through 4 for two shift types, with severity level 0 representing the in-control case and an intended overall error probability of 0.05; the authors report that RoMFCC outperformed the competing methods across the considered contamination scenarios, while functional charts performed better than charts based on scalar summaries when the Phase I sample was clean. In the real welding study, RoMFCC signaled 72.3% of the 920 Phase II observations as out of control; its estimated true detection rate was 0.723, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of [0.695, 0.753]. The corresponding reported estimates were 0.632 for the iterative functional chart, 0.541 for the non-iterative functional chart, 0.513 for the robust scalar chart, 0.462 for the iterative scalar chart, and 0.336 for the classical scalar chart. The paper reports detection rates and false alarm rates, not run lengths.

key_equations.explanation: SPE is the squared prediction error, Z is the standardized multivariate functional observation, Z-hat is its projection, H denotes the multivariate function space norm, L with subscript mon is the retained component count, xi with subscript l is a component score, and psi with subscript l is its principal component.

key_equations.name: Squared prediction error control limit

narrate.future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test the chart with autocorrelated profiles, non-normal measurements, other shift shapes, and a wider range of contamination patterns. narrate.summary: The paper studies charts for detecting a temporary change in the mean of a stream of observations, including streams with many channels. narrate.summary: The paper studies sequential monitoring for a common change in the means of many data streams that may be cross-sectionally dependent. Its main method is a direction-invariant multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) chart, which signals when the covariance-adjusted size of its smoothed observation vector exceeds a control limit. It also analyzes moving average, cumulative sum, generalized likelihood ratio, and Shiryayev-Roberts procedures, and examines thresholding and adaptive variants. The authors derive approximations for in-control average run length and detection delay, and use simulations to compare the methods. They find that MEWMA offers a practical balance across signal sizes, while hard-threshold MEWMA can improve detection for sparse signals.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 20 channels, a target in-control average run length of 1000, and a change after 100 observations, the MEWMA approximation gave in-control run lengths close to the target; the reported simulated value was 1020.5. With a signal strength of 0.5, its stationary average delay detection time was 93.65, compared with 172.78 for the moving average chart and 296.37 for the generalized likelihood ratio chart; with signal strength 2.0, the generalized likelihood ratio chart was faster, at 7.62 versus 9.86 for MEWMA. For one changed channel and signal strength 0.5, hard-threshold MEWMA reduced the reported delay from 93.65 to 66.14. The authors report that thresholding is most useful when only a small proportion of channels change, and recommend MEWMA overall for its stable performance and relatively simple design.

narrate.summary: The paper develops two-sided exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) charts for monitoring individual continuous proportions between zero and one. It considers Beta, Simplex, and Unit Gamma distributions and targets changes in the process mean in either direction, with the dispersion held fixed. The chart updates a smoothed value from each new observation and signals when that value falls outside its lower or upper control limit. The authors set the limits by simulation to achieve a chosen in-control average run length. Their simulations and an example using peanut-contamination data show that the EWMA charts can detect mean changes sooner than two-sided Shewhart charts, especially for small shifts.
narrate.key_results: For the simulations, the in-control mean was 0.2, shifts were 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, or 0.08 in either direction, and the dispersion was held fixed. With a false-alarm rate of 0.0027, the target in-control average run length was about 370.4; the authors calibrated limits using 10,000 simulated sequences. In the Beta Case 1 setting, with precision 290, a shift to 0.18 gave an average run length of 13.89 for the EWMA chart with lambda 0.05, versus 54.60 for the Shewhart chart; for a shift to 0.22, the corresponding values were 14.04 and 69.71. The authors report that for small shifts in the interval 0.18 to 0.22, the improvement in detection was 70 to 90 percent in the studied cases. In the peanut example, the Shewhart chart signaled at Phase II observation 12, while the EWMA charts signaled at observation 5 for lambda 0.05 or 0.10 and at observation 4 for lambda 0.20, about seven to eight observations earlier.

narrate.limitations_stated: The charts are developed assuming known in-control parameters and that assignable causes change only the process mean, leaving dispersion unchanged. narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulation study uses a single in-control mean of 0.2 and four selected dispersion settings, so performance beyond those settings is not established. The simulations do not assess serial dependence, and the real-data illustration is limited to 34 peanut observations, with only 14 used for Phase II monitoring.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying cases where both process parameters change and cases where parameters are unknown and must be estimated. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate these charts on more operational datasets and under serially dependent observations, with direct checks of how dependence affects false alarms and detection. It could also provide a practical method for identifying the direction or likely cause of a signal and make the reproduction code more readily accessible than by request.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces a nonparametric chart for monitoring sequential profiles, where each profile consists of quality measurements related to explanatory variables. The method monitors the leading eigenvector of a moving-window sample correlation matrix, comparing it with the direction expected when all profiles are in control. When a window contains a mix of in-control and changed profiles, its correlation structure can change and the eigenvector can move away from that expected direction. The chart signals when the largest such distance, evaluated across selected replacements with historical in-control profiles, exceeds a bootstrap-based upper control limit. Simulations and a robot-arm example show that the method can combine very long in-control run lengths with rapid detection in the studied settings.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with multiple predictors, the chart achieved an in-control average run length greater than 5 million and an out-of-control average run length of 1 across the reported scenarios. With the change point at monitoring step 30, its false alarm rate was zero; with the change point at step 10,000, the reported false alarm rates ranged from zero to 0.01, while the out-of-control average run length remained 1. Supplementary simulations reported lower bounds on the in-control average run length from 7,068,576 to 8,365,168 for the tested settings. In the robot-arm example, the chart had an out-of-control average run length of 1 in every scenario, and only 4 of 27 scenarios had positive false alarm rates, all below 0.02; the comparison chart based on principal component analysis had average detection delays of 1.46, 1.53, and 2.12 at in-control average run lengths of 200, 370, and 5,010,603, respectively.

key_equations.name: Charting statistic
key_equations.explanation: S is the monitoring statistic, K is the set of selected replacement counts, k_1 is a replacement count, v(k_1) is the leading eigenvector after replacing that many oldest profiles with historical in-control profiles, w is the window size, and 1 is the vector of ones.

key_equations.name: Bootstrap upper control limit
key_equations.explanation: U is the upper control limit, F is the fitted normal distribution function for bootstrap statistics, c specifies the upper quantile, and the estimated mean and variance of those statistics are μ̂_S and σ̂_S².

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report poorer performance when the profile sample size, historical reference sample, or signal strength is small, or when the in-control and mixed-profile correlations are difficult to distinguish. They note that changes such as an out-of-control profile proportional to the in-control profile, or differing from it only by a constant, may be hard to detect with a chart based on correlations. Performance was unsatisfactory for heavy-tailed errors with fewer than five moments, and small profile sample size combined with near-identical in-control and out-of-control functions could also lead to missed alarms.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The control limit is based on a normal distribution fitted to bootstrap monitoring statistics, so its extreme-tail accuracy—and thus the claimed very long in-control run lengths—may be sensitive to calibration error. The bootstrap procedure described in the supplement simulates normal errors and assumes fixed predictors, while the main comparative simulations also use fixed predictors and independent errors over time; performance under broader real-process conditions is therefore less established. The real-data evaluation uses one robot-arm task with a small set of historical normal profiles, limiting evidence about transfer to other applications.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the method to monitor changes not captured by correlations, including whether the profile-combination parameter equals one. They identify improving performance when the profile sample size is small, accommodating time-series correlation structures beyond the equicorrelated structure considered, and relaxing the requirement that predictors at different monitoring times be dependent.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate calibration methods that do not rely on a normal approximation for the extreme bootstrap tail, especially with heavy-tailed or serially dependent observations. Broader validation on real production streams, plus methods to identify which profiles or measurements drove a signal, would help engineers assess and act on alarms.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors high-dimensional counts indexed by location, category, and time, with disease counts and population sizes as its motivating example. Its method, Poisson Assisted Smooth Sparse Tensor Decomposition (PoSSTenD), separates the rate into a smooth global trend and sparse local hot spots. It uses a cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart of residual-based scores to signal when hot spots occur, and uses the sparse component to identify their locations and categories. The chart signals when its accumulated score exceeds a selected alarm limit. In simulations, the method detected shifts quickly under both increasing and decreasing population trends, and it signaled in 2017 in the disease-count example.
narrate.key_results: In 1,000 simulation replications, with hot spots beginning after time 15 in a 26-time-point series, PoSSTenD had an average run length after a shift (ARL1) of 2.0150 for shift size 0.05 with increasing population and 4.2780 with decreasing population. For shift size 0.2, its ARL1 was 1.0000 under both population trends. At shift size 0.2 with decreasing population, the reported localization precision was 81.13%, recall was 53.52%, and F-measure was 64.41%. For the real-data example, the authors set the average run length to false alarm (ARL0) to 50 using the first 15 years as the in-control reference period; PoSSTenD signaled in 2017. The authors report that other benchmark charts were slower or did not signal within the study period in several simulation settings, and that some could not localize hot spots.

key_equations.name: CUSUM update and alarm rule

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that localization can have a relatively high false-positive rate when hot spots are small. narrate.limitations_unstated: The model assumes Poisson counts and does not model serial dependence or extra-Poisson variation, which could affect alarm rates and detection delays in operational data. The simulations use randomly selected sparse hot spots and simplified population trends, while the real-data example is short and has no verified hot-spot ground truth; thus, the reported signal and localization accuracy have limited external validation.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest significance testing or a prespecified threshold to reduce false-positive localizations, and mention a two-sided test for detecting decreasing shifts. They also state that the method can be extended to tensors with more than three dimensions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the method with overdispersed and temporally dependent counts, and test whether its false-alarm calibration holds when the reference period is short or contains shifts. Further validation on operational datasets with independently confirmed events, and procedures to investigate or rank locations after an alarm, would help assess its usefulness to quality engineers.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes functional real-time monitoring (FRTM) for quality characteristics recorded as curves, so a process can be assessed before a curve or batch is complete. It aligns each partial curve to a reference pattern and represents both changes in curve shape or size and changes in timing. The method reduces these data using mixed functional principal component analysis (mFPCA) and monitors them with two statistics. A signal is raised when either statistic crosses its empirical control limit at a monitored time point. In simulations and a penicillin-process benchmark, the proposed method generally detected changes more effectively than the two competing methods considered.
narrate.key_results: The simulation study used two types of phase variation, three misalignment settings, three shift types, and severity levels of 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, and 1.00, with changes beginning at 30% or 60% of process duration. For the reported setting with changes beginning at 30%, each condition had 50 simulation runs, a reference sample of 500 in-control observations, and 500 out-of-control observations; the reference sample was split between model fitting and control-limit tuning. With the overall type I error probability set to 0.05, the authors report that all methods controlled the false alarm rate near its nominal level, while FRTM had higher detection rates across the considered simulation settings; detection was generally weaker for more complex phase variation and for changes beginning later. The penicillin benchmark included four datasets, each with 400 normal-operation batches, and 15 fault types with 50 repetitions for each dataset, fault type, and magnitude; FRTM had the highest mean detection rate in almost all reported comparisons for dissolved oxygen and base flow rate. The paper reports no run-length results.

key_equations.name: Squared prediction error

key_equations.name: Empirical control limits

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify estimation uncertainty in the warping components and the choice of mFPCA weights as issues for further development. They also note that extending the approach to multivariate functional data presents methodological and computational challenges.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The control charts and component model are estimated from a finite reference sample, but the paper does not quantify how uncertainty in those estimates affects false alarms or detection. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to multivariate functional data. They also propose incorporating uncertainty in estimated warping components into dimensionality reduction and developing a criterion for choosing the mFPCA weights.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test calibration and detection on operating production data with realistic temporal dependence, measurement noise, and process variation. Research could also add signal interpretation or fault-diagnosis procedures to help engineers determine what part of a curve and which phase or amplitude component caused an alarm.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Angular Control Chart for monitoring times to failure in multi-state systems, both overall and for individual state transitions. It assumes a fully repairable system with major failures, where each failure returns the system to its perfect-functioning state. The chart places each observed time on its state line and represents it by an angle determined by the observation and that state’s median time to failure. An observation outside the angular control-limit band signals a possible reliability change: a longer time to failure indicates improvement, while a shorter time indicates degradation. Simulated examples illustrate the chart for several probability distributions, but the paper does not report formal run-length performance results.
narrate.key_results: The authors use an acceptable false-alarm probability of 0.27% for their control limits. In Example I, the first 25 simulated observations were in control; for the next 25, the exponential scale parameters changed from 100, 400, and 800 to 400, 200, and 200 for the three transitions. The chart showed two improvement signals for the first transition, one degradation signal for the third, and no individual out-of-control signals for the second, although 11 of its 17 points were above the center line. In Example II, accumulating times to failure over every two failures produced one out-of-control point for the first transition, compared with two in Example I; in Example III, 33 of 50 points were above the center line after scale parameters changed, indicating overall improvement in that simulated example.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a variable sampling interval (VSI) multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) chart for monitoring compositional data (CoDa), whose components are constrained to sum to a constant. It first applies the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation so the chart can monitor unconstrained coordinates of the compositions. The chart uses a MEWMA statistic and takes samples at a long interval when the statistic is in a safe region, or a short interval when it is in a warning region; it signals when the control limit is exceeded. The authors use a Markov-chain approach to calculate time to signal and choose chart settings. In their numerical comparisons, the proposed chart signals sooner than the fixed sampling interval (FSI) MEWMA chart for the tested shifts and settings.
narrate.key_results: The comparisons used sample size 1, 3-part compositions, an in-control average time to signal (ATS) of 200, and an in-control average sampling interval of 1. Shift sizes ranged from 0.25 to 2.00, and the short sampling interval was either 0.1 or 0.5. At shift size 0.25, the FSI chart had an average run length of 64.6, compared with an ATS of 56.8 for the proposed chart with short interval 0.1; with short interval 0.5, its ATS was 63.5. At shift size 0.50, the proposed chart's ATS was 19.9 with short interval 0.1 and 23.5 with short interval 0.5, compared with an FSI average run length of 26.4. The paper reports that the proposed chart outperformed the FSI chart across the tested shifts, with smaller gains for shifts of 1.75 and 2.00.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors the proportion of non-conforming products when recorded product status may be wrong because of misclassification. It proposes correcting the observed sample proportion using the assumed misclassification probabilities, then smoothing the corrected proportions with an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart. The chart signals when its statistic reaches or exceeds an upper control limit; the lower control limit is zero. Its limits are asymmetric and are designed to work with small samples. The simulations show that correction makes detection performance close to that obtained when the true product statuses are observed, whereas using the uncorrected data can delay signals.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, the authors set the in-control average run length (ARL) to 370 and studied sample sizes of 5, 10, 15, and 20, smoothing parameters of 0.05 and 0.2, and increases in the non-conforming proportion of 10% and 20%. Across the reported settings, corrected out-of-control ARL values were generally close to values based on true statuses, while the naive chart often had longer ARLs; for example, with in-control proportion 0.05, sample size 5, a 10% increase, and classification probability 0.95, the true-status, naive, and corrected ARLs were 208.0, 251.9, and 207.7, respectively. In the orange juice example, the observed in-control proportion was 0.111, and correction under classification probabilities 0.95 and 0.99 gave corrected proportions of 0.068 and 0.103; the chart signaled an in-control point under one setting, which the authors identify as a false alarm. For the out-of-control samples in that example, the corrected chart detected the shift under the displayed smoothing parameters and misclassification settings, while the naive chart missed the second point in one displayed setting.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a method for simultaneously monitoring many categorical data streams, including nominal categories and ordered categories. For nominal streams it detects changes in category probabilities, and for ordinal streams it detects location shifts in an assumed latent continuous variable. It calculates a local likelihood-ratio statistic for each stream, smooths it over time, and transforms the local results to a common scale before combining them with a goodness-of-fit statistic. The chart signals when the global statistic exceeds a control limit. Simulations generally show that the method performs well against two comparison methods, and a semiconductor example signals a change at sample 22.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors a univariate sequence that moves from a baseline distribution to a changed distribution for an unknown period, then returns to baseline. It uses likelihood-based cumulative sum (CUSUM) statistics to detect both the onset of a change and the return to baseline, and estimates the endpoints of each changed interval. A signal occurs when a CUSUM statistic crosses a threshold; the method restarts its statistics after detected changes and readjustments. The main finding is that, when the distributions are known, the thresholds can control the probability of any false alarm and any false readjustment at preselected levels, even when the number of transient changes is unknown. The paper also gives an asymptotic false-alarm bound for a generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) version with estimated parameters.
narrate.key_results: For known baseline and changed distributions, the authors show that the largest CUSUM value gives the likelihood-ratio statistic and that its threshold can limit the false alarm probability to the selected level alpha. For multiple transient changes with unknown count, their restarted procedures control the familywise false alarm rate at alpha and the familywise false readjustment rate at beta, without requiring a correction based on the number of changes. For the GLR procedure, under the paper's exponential-family and segment-length conditions, the false alarm probability by time n to the power omega is at most alpha plus a term that tends to zero as n increases. The paper presents asymptotic localization results for change-point estimates but reports no numerical run lengths, simulation rankings, or numerical performance comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper studies cost-optimal monitoring of a single process characteristic when shifts are positive and their sizes can follow a mixture distribution. narrate.summary: The paper compares charts for monitoring a process mean using independent, normally distributed individual observations, with known and constant in-control variability. It examines synthetic-type charts, which signal after two out-of-limit observations occur sufficiently close together, and EWMA charts, which signal when a smoothed statistic crosses a limit. The paper evaluates how quickly charts signal for changes occurring at different times, emphasizing steady-state performance as well as performance when a change happens at the start of monitoring. In the study, the EWMA chart generally performs better, particularly for small shifts, and the author cautions that head-start synthetic charts can look unusually effective when assessed only from the start of monitoring. narrate.summary: The paper monitors changes in the transition probabilities of a serially correlated directed network, using metro passenger flows as its motivating example. It converts transition counts into row-standardized transition probabilities and applies a spring-length-based method to reduce the effect of short-range serial correlation without specifying a parametric time-series model. It runs a cumulative sum control chart on each row and combines the row statistics using weights based on the number of transitions from each node. The chart signals when this weighted statistic exceeds a control limit. Simulations and a metro traffic example show that the proposed chart is generally more robust to serial correlation while retaining useful sensitivity to mean shifts.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used 10,000 replications and calibrated charts to an in-control average run length of approximately 200; the maximum spring length was set to 4. In the scenario where both transition probabilities and transition totals were serially correlated, with initial node totals of 100 and 500, reducing the first-row mean transition probability from 0.45 to 0.44 gave the proposed weighted chart an average run length of 71.01 and a standard deviation of run length of 47.29. In the metro example, the proposed chart signaled at the fourth observation during Phase II monitoring, as did the un-decorrelated top-one cumulative sum chart; the decorrelated chart monitoring transition probabilities signaled at the nineteenth observation, while the other two comparison charts did not show sustained increases under the shift. In Phase I back-testing, the proposed chart did not signal on the selected in-control data, whereas the un-decorrelated cumulative sum and exponentially weighted moving average charts signaled.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a Phase I method for screening individual observations from high-dimensional processes when the historical sample is smaller than the number of variables and may contain outliers. It monitors changes in the process mean using a distance based on variable-specific variances, rather than requiring estimation of the full covariance matrix. Robust reweighted estimates are used for the in-control parameters, and a distributional adjustment is applied to the charting statistic. An observation signals when its adjusted statistic exceeds an upper threshold determined by the chosen false-alarm probability. Simulations and two data examples show that the method can detect contaminated observations and mean shifts under the studied conditions.
narrate.key_results: For sample size 200 and dimensions 30 to 100, the simulated false-alarm rates with the adjustment were 0.009 to 0.013 for a target of 0.01, and 0.047 to 0.060 for a target of 0.05 across the two simulated covariance scenarios. Without the adjustment, the corresponding rates were 0.015 to 0.036 and 0.057 to 0.091. In the comparison with the minimum covariance determinant method, at a target false-alarm rate of 0.05 and a contamination rate of 0.1, the proposed method's Type I error was close to 0.05 while the comparator's was almost 0.25; the proposed method also had greater detection power, particularly at dimension 100. In the wooden-board example, with 24 profiles and 314 measurements per profile, profile 6 was flagged at a threshold corresponding to 0.005, and profiles 3, 6, and 16 were identified for investigation across the thresholds considered. In the breast cancer example, the chart indicated a shift after observation 357 at a threshold corresponding to 0.05; the data had 30 variables, with 357 benign observations followed by 212 malignant observations.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors contours of additive-manufactured products, represented as functional curves from two-dimensional slices of three-dimensional shapes. Its method separates variation into translation, amplitude, and phase components, then constructs a functional boxplot for each component. A product signals as an outlying curve when its distance from the component median exceeds the cutoff set by the boxplot extremes. The authors tested the approach using simulated deformations of a benchmark shape and four shapes from the Thingi10K model database. They report that the method identified the deliberately deformed products in many scenarios, while also flagging some products generated from the nominal distributions.
narrate.key_results: Each simulation used 150 samples. For the benchmark shape, the surface-roughness scenario detected the two deliberately roughened products; in the amplitude scenario, two amplitude outliers and one translation outlier were detected, with one product flagged in both and none flagged for phase; in the phase scenario, four products were detected. For the four Thingi10K shapes, the numbers detected in the roughness scenario were 4, 3, 4, and 5, respectively, for the spiral bevel gear, wheel, logo, and coin loading tube; the corresponding counts were 7, 4, 4, and 5 for the amplitude scenario, and 3, 7, 2, and 3 for the phase scenario. The paper reports no run-length results or calibrated false-alarm probabilities.

key_equations.name: Outlier signal rule
key_equations.explanation: The chart signals when d, the curve's distance from the median for a component, exceeds c, the cutoff determined from that component's boxplot whisker extremes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the method is designed for smooth functions, although their roughness simulation suggests it can also work with nonsmooth curves. They also state that when separate functional approximations for the two in-plane coordinates are not suitable, representing the whole geometry as a large data cloud can make computation intensive.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses constructed simulation scenarios rather than measurements from an operating production process, so its detection performance under real process variation is not established. The results depend on a finite reference sample of 150 curves, but the paper does not quantify how reference-sample estimation affects cutoff stability or report calibrated false-alarm probabilities across repeated trials. The analysis concerns individual slice contours and does not assess dependence between successive products or layers.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a multivariate functional outlier method for more intricate shapes that cannot safely be represented by separate coordinate functions, extending the analysis from layer contours to surfaces. They also propose theoretical work on the method's asymptotic properties.
narrate.future_work_unstated: The method should be validated on real production data and across different manufacturing processes, with false-alarm behavior and detection rates reported under realistic baseline conditions. Further work could assess sequential dependence across products and layers, and provide diagnostic guidance for locating or explaining the source of a detected deformation.

narrate.summary: This paper reviews and critiques process-monitoring charts that combine or recursively reuse familiar chart statistics. It evaluates five examples for detecting shifts in the mean of independent, normally distributed observations when the process standard deviation is known. The charts signal when a running statistic crosses a control limit, or when a specified runs rule is met. The authors compare signal performance not only for shifts present at startup, but also for shifts that occur after monitoring has begun. Their main finding is that carefully matched conventional charts generally perform as well as or better than the more complicated compound charts, especially for later changes.
narrate.key_results: For the mixed EWMA-CUSUM chart, comparisons used an in-control ARL of 170 and shifts of 0.5 and 1.5; a suitably tuned CUSUM had lower or similar delay at shift 0.5 and dominated the mixed chart at shift 1.5. For the double moving average study, with in-control ARL 370, the EWMA had the lowest steady-state ARL across shifts in the displayed comparisons, including designs chosen for shifts of 0.6 and 1.5. For the double EWMA comparison, with in-control ARL 200, the reported shift values were expressed as delta divided by the square root of five: at shift value 1, the steady-state ARL was 6.3 for the double EWMA and 4.0 for the EWMA; at shift value 2, it was 4.1 and 2.2, respectively. For the double progressive mean comparison, also with in-control ARL 200, the zero-state ARL at shift 0.75 was 8.05 for the double progressive mean and 8.99 for the EWMA with smoothing parameter 0.05, but the paper's delay profiles show that the double progressive mean performed substantially worse for changes occurring at time 30 or later.

narrate.summary: Hybrid variable monitoring (HVM) monitors continuous and binary process variables together using data collected during healthy operation. It models continuous variables with Gaussian distributions and binary variables with Bernoulli distributions, combining their probabilities in a weighted score. The method squares the log probability score to form a monitoring statistic and estimates a control limit using kernel density estimation (KDE). A sample is flagged when its statistic reaches or exceeds that limit. The authors report improved detection with relatively low false alarm rates in a simulation and in a thermal power plant fan-system case.
narrate.key_results: In the numerical study, 4,000 healthy samples were used for training and 4,000 samples for testing, with the fault starting at sample 2,001; the authors ran 100 independent repetitions. In experiment II, HVM had a mean false alarm rate of 0.60% and a mean fault detection rate of 94.73%, while the best fault detection rate among the compared traditional methods using continuous variables was 6.47%. In experiment I, HVM’s mean false alarm rate was 0.62% and its mean fault detection rate was 52.34%. In the fan-system case, 35 continuous and 35 binary variables were sampled every 5 seconds; using 1,000 healthy samples for modeling, HVM achieved a 4.2% false alarm rate and a 100% fault detection rate.

narrate.summary: This review examines process-monitoring methods that use auxiliary information-based (AIB) estimates, in which a correlated auxiliary characteristic helps estimate the quality characteristic of interest. The methods generally assume that a parameter of the auxiliary characteristic, such as its mean, is known and remains unchanged over time. The review describes univariate and multivariate methods, with particular attention to Shewhart and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) charts. A chart signals when its statistic crosses a control limit, but changes in the auxiliary characteristic can cause false alarms or hide changes in the quality characteristic. The authors conclude that these strong assumptions make AIB methods risky for quality-control applications and warn against their use.
narrate.key_results: The authors calibrated the Shewhart and EWMA charts to an in-control average run length (ARL) of 200 and used 50,000 simulation runs. When the quality characteristic remained in control and the auxiliary mean shifted by the standardized amount 1 at correlation 0.75, the reported ARL was 21.3 for the Shewhart chart and 7.3 for the EWMA chart with smoothing parameter 0.10. In a masking example with correlation 0.5 and a quality-characteristic shift of size 2, the EWMA chart did not signal through time 200; if the auxiliary mean had remained in control, the shift would have been signaled after an average of 3.3 samples. The results demonstrate that auxiliary-variable changes can greatly increase false alarms and can completely mask a shift in the quality characteristic.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper's demonstrations focus on mean shifts in bivariate normal data and examine two charts based on the difference estimator; they do not establish how often the reported effects occur across the full range of AIB methods reviewed. The simulations do not test violations such as non-normality, changing variance or correlation, or estimated model parameters, and the paper provides no real-process validation of its critique.

Real-process validation and methods for diagnosing the cause of a signal would help compare AIB charts with profile monitoring, cause-selecting charts, and other alternatives.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors multivariate industrial time series, including measurements from a three-phase flow facility and a medium-speed coal mill. Its proposed probabilistic predictable feature analysis (PPFA) models temporal relationships among latent variables while accounting for measurement noise. It uses T-squared and squared prediction error (SPE) to flag unusual latent values and model residuals, and adds the Dynamic Index (DI) to identify changes in process dynamics. A sample is flagged when a statistic exceeds its control limit, which the method estimates using kernel density estimation. In the studied cases, the authors report that PPFA detected faults earlier or more informatively than the two deterministic comparison methods.
narrate.key_results: For the three-phase flow facility, the model was trained on 3,200 normal samples and evaluated at a 99% confidence level. In the airline-blockage case, the fault ran from sample 657 to sample 3,777; PPFA's T-squared and SPE statistics exceeded their limits at about sample 1,267, and DI showed peaks near samples 2,760, 3,067, and 3,777. For the coal mill, the training set contained 2,385 normal samples; in the mechanical-failure case, PPFA detected the fault occurring from sample 94 to sample 452, while the comparison method's statistics first exceeded their limits around sample 110. In the coal-blockage case, which ran from sample 195 to sample 435, the paper reports a delay of nearly 100 samples, or 0.56 hour, for the comparison method, while PPFA's T-squared and SPE signalled when the fault occurred.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors the dynamics of batch-process measurements by fitting an autoregressive moving average model separately to each historical in-control batch. A multivariate Hotelling chart checks whether a new batch's estimated coefficients differ from the reference pattern, while individual Student charts help identify the coefficient associated with a signal. The charts use adjusted distributions that account for variation among the estimated coefficients from the reference batches. In simulations, the multivariate chart detected changes to dynamic coefficients faster than the residual-based comparison, though that comparison was better for some changes in the process mean. A public engine-noise dataset also showed that the multivariate chart could detect many batches from the alternative condition, including when relatively few reference batches were used.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with a 1% false alarm setting, 30 reference batches, and batch length 100, changing the autoregressive coefficient from 0.2 to 0.6 gave a mean run length of 1.30 batches for the proposed chart, compared with 7.26 for the residual chart. For the moving-average coefficient, changing it from 0.5 to 0.8 under the same settings gave mean run lengths of 2.16 and 70.07 batches, respectively. For an intercept change from 1 to 0.8, with 100 reference batches and length 200, the proposed chart's mean run length was 16.60, compared with 1.13 for the residual chart, showing that the advantage did not extend to every mean change. In the engine-noise example, with 500 reference batches and a 1% false alarm setting, the reported false alarm rate was 0.02 and the detection rate for batches in the alternative group was 0.70; with 10 reference batches, those rates were 0.03 and 0.31.

narrate.summary: The paper studies a Shewhart chart for monitoring the ratio of two normally distributed quality characteristics when measurements are autocorrelated over time. It models the paired measurements with a first-order bivariate autoregressive model and accounts for that dependence when calculating the distribution of subgroup ratios. The chart plots each subgroup’s ratio of sample means and signals when the plotted value falls outside probability-based control limits. The authors find that autocorrelation generally increases detection delays compared with independent observations, particularly for small process shifts. A simulated food-recipe example illustrates the chart’s use for monitoring the ratio of pumpkin seeds to flaxseeds.
narrate.key_results: The performance study set the in-control average run length at 200, corresponding to a false alarm probability of 0.005, and examined subgroup sizes from 2 to 15, coefficients of variation of 0.01 or 0.2, and autocorrelation coefficients of 0.1 or 0.7. For subgroup size 5, coefficients of variation of 0.01 for both variables, correlation of negative 0.8, and a ratio shift factor of 0.99, the out-of-control average run length was 23.1 with autocorrelation coefficients of 0.1, 59.7 with coefficients of 0.7, and 19.1 without autocorrelation. The results generally show longer detection delays as autocorrelation increases; the authors also report poor detection of small shifts when both coefficients of variation are high. In the food example, a simulated 2% ratio increase produced control limits of 0.9723582 and 1.0284276, and the chart signaled at samples 14 and 15; the chart designed without accounting for autocorrelation signaled at sample 12.

key_equations.name: Charting statistic
key_equations.explanation: At time i, the plotted statistic Z-bar is the ratio of the sample means X-bar and Y-bar, calculated from n paired observations indexed by j.

key_equations.name: Probability control limits
key_equations.explanation: The lower and upper limits are quantiles of the ratio distribution; F_Z inverse is its inverse cumulative distribution function, alpha is the target false alarm probability, and the gamma, omega, and rho terms describe the variation, standard-deviation ratio, and correlation of the subgroup means.

key_equations.name: Miss probability and out-of-control average run length
key_equations.explanation: Beta is the probability of a plotted ratio falling between the limits under the shifted process distribution, F_Z is that distribution’s cumulative distribution function, and ARL subscript 1 is the out-of-control average run length.

narrate.limitations_stated: The analysis assumes a diagonal autoregressive coefficient matrix, so it excludes lagged dependence between one variable and the other. It also assumes sampling intervals are long enough that successive subgroup-ratio statistics are independent, even though observations within each subgroup are autocorrelated. The authors state that their ratio-quantile approximation is considered accurate for coefficients of variation in the range from 0 to 0.2.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The performance calculations use specified process parameters, so they do not establish how parameter estimation from finite reference data affects the control limits or detection results. The food example uses simulated measurements rather than an operational production dataset, and the study does not test robustness to non-normal measurements or dependence between the variables across time lags.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose designing more advanced ratio charts to reduce autocorrelation’s negative effect, studying autocorrelation effects on the exponentially weighted moving average ratio chart, and implementing ratio charts with Phase I data.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a bivariate time-between-event (BTBE) chart for monitoring two related event times that arrive at different times. It detects changes in event-time distributions by plotting each observed event as soon as it occurs, rather than waiting for a complete pair. The chart uses event-specific, dynamic control limits and signals when a plotted value crosses a limit; its signal also identifies which event time triggered the alarm. The authors derive control limits and average time to signal (ATS) expressions, then evaluate the method through simulations, comparison with an existing chart, and an AIDS data example. The results show that avoiding the wait for a paired event can improve detection, particularly when the two event times have unequal expectations or when shifts are large.
narrate.key_results: The simulation study targeted an in-control ATS of 200. For independent data with equal expectations of 5, increasing only the first event-time expectation by 50% produced an ATS of 110.5 for the BTBE chart, while increasing both expectations by 50% produced an ATS of 79.7. In the comparison with the multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) chart, for unequal in-control expectations of 5 and 15, a 50% increase in both expectations gave ATS values of 103.1 for BTBE and 126.6 for MEWMA with smoothing parameter 0.1; for the scenario with dependent event times and shifted expectations of 10 and 30, the corresponding results were 83.2 and 100.8. The study also reports that MEWMA with smoothing parameter 0.1 could be quicker for small shifts when expectations were equal, while BTBE performed better for large shifts and generally for unequal expectations. In the AIDS example, using adults as the in-control reference and children as shifted data, the chart signaled five times on the first event time; the authors set the target in-control ATS to 25 for this application.

narrate.summary: The paper examines charts for monitoring changes in a process mean, focusing on the generally weighted moving average (GWMA) chart and comparing it with the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart. The GWMA method weights current and past observations, but its weights can give relatively more emphasis to past data and do not always decline regularly with age. A signal occurs when the chart statistic falls outside its control limits. The authors argue that GWMA statistics lack a recursive calculation and the Markov property, making calculation and performance assessment more demanding than for EWMA charts. Their comparisons find that suitably tuned EWMA charts perform as well as or better than the studied GWMA charts in most reported comparisons.
narrate.key_results: For the comparisons with q equal to 0.75, the in-control average run length (ARL) was about 500 for the charts. At a mean shift of 0.5 standard deviations, the GWMA chart with alpha equal to 0.5 had a zero-state ARL of 40.76, while its variance-matched EWMA chart with lambda equal to 0.152 had an ARL of 34.60; at a shift of 1 standard deviation, the corresponding values were 11.74 and 8.90. Across the reported zero-state comparisons, that EWMA design had lower ARL than all the considered GWMA designs. In steady-state comparisons, the GWMA chart with alpha equal to 0.5 had slightly lower ARL for shifts greater than 2 standard deviations, while the matched EWMA performed better for shifts up to 2 standard deviations. The authors used 10^8 simulation replications for conditional expected delays and used the delay at time 100 as a substitute for the steady-state value.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors event times and node identities in mutually exciting network point processes, modeled as Hawkes processes. It proposes a recursive cumulative sum (CUSUM) method to detect abrupt changes in the event interactions, including changes in network influence parameters. The method evaluates likelihood evidence for candidate change times and signals when the largest evidence value crosses a chosen threshold. A kernel truncation option reduces memory use, while updates on a time grid reduce computation. In the reported simulations, the proposed method detected changes more effectively and ran faster than the compared score, generalized likelihood ratio (GLR), and Shewhart-type methods.
narrate.key_results: For simulated networks of 8 and 100 nodes, the CUSUM with correctly specified post-change parameters had the best reported expected detection delay (EDD) versus average run length (ARL) performance, followed by the score method and then the GLR; all three outperformed the Shewhart baseline. Over a time horizon of 50000, reported computation times for the 8-node network were 1.508 seconds for CUSUM, 37.14 for GLR, 3.013 for the score method, and 0.046 for Shewhart; for the 100-node network they were 1.304, 54.89, 12.71, and 0.030 seconds, respectively. In the 80-node simulated neural network example, CUSUM took 0.44 seconds, compared with 32.48 seconds for GLR and 4.63 seconds for the score method. The theoretical analysis gives a lower bound of approximately one half of the exponential of the threshold for the expected number of events before an alarm under no change; the paper presents the EDD relationship to threshold divided by asymptotic divergence as an expected result, not a general proved result.

narrate.summary: The method monitors changes in the transmission, progression, recovery, and mortality parameters of a time-varying SEIRD model. It updates Bayesian parameter estimates from new daily infection, recovery, and death data using an augmented particle sampling procedure. The chart smooths the mean changes in these four parameters with a MEWMA statistic and signals when its squared multivariate statistic exceeds the stated threshold of 9.48. The authors demonstrate the method on public COVID-19 data for Qatar. In that example, the chart identified several periods of parameter change that the authors linked to visible changes in the epidemic data and government interventions.
narrate.key_results: For Qatar, the authors used 1,000 posterior samples at each time and a smoothing coefficient of 0.2; the chart signaled on days 40, 44, 47, 64, 65, 67, 68, 69, 71, 77, 95, and 123, using 9.48 as the threshold. The first signal was around day 40, after the process had appeared stable through day 40; later signals coincided with volatility in estimated transmission and recovery rates and with changes in active infections. With smoothing coefficient 0.1, signals occurred on days 44, 47, 69, 77, and 123, while 0.15 also missed day 95; coefficients of 0.25 gave the same signal days as 0.2, and 0.3 added signals on days 72, 74, and 80. The reported fit statistic was 0.9999, while 0.8394 of observations fell within the 95% posterior predictive bands, which the authors said indicated that the model represented less uncertainty than it should.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a structural health monitoring method for operational wind turbine blades. narrate.summary: The paper proposes a chart for detecting sparse changes in the mean of high-dimensional data, including data with unequal variances or unknown distributions. It compares the means of observations before and after candidate change points within a moving window, then takes the largest variable-level difference. The chart signals when this largest statistic exceeds a control limit calibrated by bootstrap to a predefined false alarm probability. A signal also gives an estimated change point, and the authors describe a post-signal procedure to identify suspicious variables. Simulations and a semiconductor benchmark example show that the method can detect large sparse shifts without requiring a large reference sample before monitoring begins.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 100 variables, a window of 40 observations, and a change point at observation 25, for a shift size of 1 the detection probabilities were 0.508 and 0.822 for 10% and 25% changed variables under the baseline model; under the heteroscedastic model they were 0.408 and 0.712. For a shift size of 1.5, the baseline detection probability was 1 for both sparsity levels, with conditional expected detection delays of 15 observations; at shift size 2, detection probability was 1 under the heteroscedastic model as well. With shift size 2, the post-signal procedure correctly identified about 80% of changed variables in the simulation settings reported. In the semiconductor example, detection probability was 1 for all reported window sizes of 20, 30, and 40 and change points of 10, 25, and 50; the control limits were set using a false alarm probability of 0.01.

narrate.summary: The paper revisits the g and h charts, which monitor the number of conforming cases between consecutive nonconformities. The g chart follows subgroup totals, while the h chart follows subgroup averages. A signal occurs when a subgroup value falls above the upper control limit or below the lower control limit. narrate.summary: The paper studies an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart for monitoring the variance of normally distributed process measurements when the in-control (IC) variance must be estimated from preliminary data. The chart detects increases with an upper limit, or increases and decreases with two limits, by signaling when the EWMA of sample variances crosses a limit. Instead of calibrating the chart by its average run length, the method sets limits to achieve a chosen probability of a false alarm within a specified monitoring horizon. Numerical algorithms calculate the resulting limits while accounting for uncertainty in the preliminary estimate. The paper finds that this approach gives more suitable false alarm calibration, but that small variance changes can be difficult to detect when the preliminary sample is small.
narrate.key_results: In the main examples, the subgroup size was five, the monitoring horizon was 1,000 samples, and the target probability of a false alarm by that horizon was 0.25. For the upper chart with smoothing constant lambda equal to 0.1 and 50 preliminary samples, the reported out-of-control average run length was 84.8 for a standard deviation 1.2 times the in-control level, and 9.52 for a standard deviation 1.5 times that level. In the two-sided chart under the same settings, the reported in-control average run length was 6,803; for the upper chart it exceeded 800,000. The authors recommend at least 50 preliminary samples when detecting small changes, and suggest smoothing constants of 0.1 or 0.2 for general use.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors geometric changes in manufactured three-dimensional parts by tracking the leading Laplace-Beltrami (LB) eigenvalues estimated from scans. A distribution-free multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (DFEWMA) chart uses ranks of the eigenvalues and signals when its combined statistic crosses a control threshold. The eigenvalue profiles can be compared without registering parts or requiring scans to have matching numbers of points. In simulations, the FEM-based charts detected many defects in about two sampled parts while maintaining the specified in-control run length, and generally outperformed the earlier localized Laplacian approach.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a chart for monitoring dependent multivariate process measurements when their joint distribution is unknown, focusing on the bivariate case. narrate.summary: The paper introduces a method that combines orthogonal locality preserving projection (OLPP) with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to monitor multivariate process measurements. MLE estimates the intrinsic dimensionality (ID), and OLPP projects the measurements into a lower-dimensional space that preserves local data structure. The method monitors both variation in that projected space and reconstruction error in the residual space, using kernel density estimation (KDE) to set thresholds. A signal occurs if either statistic exceeds its threshold; observations below both thresholds are treated as fault-free. In numerical, reactor, and Tennessee Eastman simulations, the method generally detects the tested faults effectively and compares favorably with the selected monitoring methods.
narrate.key_results: In the numerical example, the authors report fault detection rates (FDRs) near 100% and false alarm rates (FARs) below 5% for three injected faults. For the continuous stirred-tank reactor cases, the method's FDR was 99.80% for Fault 4 and 83.19% for Fault 5, with a normal-operation FAR of 0.50%. In the Tennessee Eastman benchmark, the reported FAR was 0.63%; FDRs were 99.75% for IDV(1), 99.88% for IDV(12), and 100% for IDV(14). Across all 21 benchmark faults, the authors report the best overall trade-off between FDR and FAR for their method, while noting that detection remained poor for some faults and that the result for IDV(19) was not better than several alternatives.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors nonlinear processes using multivariate sensor measurements collected during normal operation. Its improved mixture of probabilistic principal component analysis (I-MPPCA) fits multiple local probabilistic principal component models and combines their results using the probability that each measurement belongs to each local model. The method combines Hotelling’s T-squared statistic and squared prediction error into a composite statistic, and also offers weighted global statistics across the local models. A signal occurs when a statistic exceeds a threshold estimated from normal-operation data using kernel density estimation. Simulations on the Tennessee Eastman process and an autosuspension model show that the method can reduce the number of charts and perform well, including when measurements are missing.
narrate.key_results: For the Tennessee Eastman simulation, the authors used 960 normal training samples and 960 test samples, comprising 160 normal samples followed by 800 faulty samples; the model used 6 principal components and 6 local models, with a confidence level of 0.99. Across the tested Tennessee Eastman faults, the reported false alarm rate was 2.5% for the proposed composite statistic, compared with 7.5% for the traditional mixture approach; missed-alarm rates varied by fault and were not uniformly lower. In the autosuspension simulations with complete data, the proposed method had a 0% missed-alarm rate for both tested faults and a 0% false-alarm rate; with missing data, its false-alarm rate was 0.47%, and its missed-alarm rates were 0.62%, 0.45%, 1.86%, and 3.15% for the four tests with 5% or 10% missing data. The authors report that the method reduced monitoring from multiple local charts to a single global composite chart and was less affected by missing values than the three compared methods.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a hybrid approach for monitoring a changing graph, using a control chart to detect changes and a graph convolutional network to classify their possible causes. Its simulated example represents ambulance stations, patients, and roads, and monitors daily response-time quantiles. The chart signals when a quadratic statistic based on the 80% and 95% response-time quantiles exceeds its control limit. After a signal, the network model classifies conditions as stable or as involving staff shortage, construction work, or traffic jams. narrate.summary: The paper monitors a panel of noisy, serially correlated time series whose means and variances can change over time, without requiring known in-control series or a specified data distribution. It identifies relatively stable series in the panel, uses them to estimate the in-control patterns, and standardizes each series before monitoring it with a cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart calibrated by block bootstrap (BB). A signal occurs when either cumulative sum statistic crosses its corresponding control limit. Support vector machine (SVM) procedures then estimate the size and classify the form of the detected shift, including jumps, trends, and oscillating shifts. In sunspot observations, the method detected previously identified major deviations as well as smaller shifts, and its simulated shift-form classifier achieved 86% accuracy on its validation set.
narrate.key_results: For the sunspot application, the authors selected a moderately stable reference pool of 12 stations and a very stable pool of 6 stations from a panel of 21 observatories. They set the smallest shift of interest to 1.5 standardized units and calibrated the two-sided CUSUM chart for an in-control average run length (ARL) of 200; the reported control limits were 8.5 and -8.5, with allowance parameter 0.75. On the SVM validation set, shift-form classification accuracy was 86%; shift-size estimation had a reported mean absolute percentage error of 26 and normalized root mean squared error of 0.26. In simulations with complex autocorrelation, the block-bootstrap chart calibrated the false-alarm rate more reliably than the parametric comparison, while for data generated by an ARMA(1,1) model the parametric approach performed better and the bootstrap results were close.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors healthcare costs and related measures, such as treatment use and condition prevalence, across hierarchical views of claims data. It uses statistical process control (SPC) to detect increasing or decreasing changes in these measures and uses a cumulative sum (CUSUM) charting approach that can account for multiple change points. Thresholds are learned using simulated data to target a false alarm rate, with reporting rules determining when detected changes are reported. The method also decomposes cost changes into contributing factors and estimates population-level utilization offsets between comparable treatments. In a case study of one million enrollees, it surfaced examples including sharp increases in Glumetza price, Coxsackie and ECHO infection costs, and hospital outpatient chemotherapy costs.
narrate.key_results: The case study used a random sample of one million enrollees and analyzed yearly data from 2013 to 2016; the paper reports no numerical run-length results or evaluations at specified shift sizes. For Glumetza, the reported cost-change rate reached 262% in 2015, while its price-change rate reached 369%; by 2016, the use impact had fallen by 82% and the total cost impact was negative. The total cost of Coxsackie and ECHO infections increased 371% in 2016, with the reported prevalence change reaching 186%. Hospital outpatient chemotherapy administration cost increased 40.8% in 2015, while the corresponding office-setting cost decreased 13.8%; the estimated Glumetza-to-Trulicity offset was associated with a cost decrease of 0.38 per member per month.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors changing networks by first representing each network with a small set of model parameters or network statistics from a temporal exponential random graph model (TERGM). It applies multivariate cumulative sum (MCUSUM) and multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) charts to detect changes in the expected values of those characteristics. A chart signals when its statistic reaches or exceeds an upper control limit calibrated by simulation to account for dependence in the monitored estimates. Simulations examine persistent changes and one-time events, and an application monitors daily United States flight networks. Both charts identify unusual flight-network behavior, including sustained signals associated with the coronavirus pandemic in 2020.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, the authors used 250 repetitions, placed the change at time 101, and calibrated charts for an in-control average run length (ARL) of 50. For a moderate one-time change that converted 0.01 of asymmetric edges into mutual edges, the best reported conditional expected delay (CED) using parameter estimates with a window of 7 was 5.52 for the MCUSUM chart and 3.16 for the MEWMA chart; using averaged network statistics, the corresponding best delays were 23.20 and 17.83. For a larger one-time change of 0.05, some MEWMA configurations detected the change with a CED of 1.00. narrate.summary: The paper monitors daily functional profiles of pollutant concentrations using a typical profile estimated from reference data. It represents each profile as a possible amplitude and phase deformation of that typical shape. The proposed Exponentially Weighted Fréchet Moving Average (EWFMA) method first checks whether a profile’s underlying shape has changed, then checks whether its deformation from the typical profile is unusual. The charts smooth the shape and deformation deviances over successive profiles and compare them with limits estimated from the in-control reference profiles. In the Athens air-quality example, the combined method correctly classified between 82.58% and 95.86% of test profiles, depending on the pollutant.
narrate.key_results: The real-data analysis used hourly pollutant measurements, with in-control profiles from 2001–2004 used for training and profiles from 2005–2007 used for testing; the analysis focused on October, November, and December. Across the combined shape and deformation monitoring stages, total classification accuracy was 87.22% for carbon monoxide, 82.58% for nitrogen dioxide, 88.35% for ozone, and 95.86% for sulfur dioxide. The method correctly identified 100% of the out-of-control cases for carbon monoxide, ozone, and sulfur dioxide, while the rate was 78.26% for nitrogen dioxide; the reported in-control classification rates were 82.56%, 82.99%, 88.30%, and 94.79%, respectively. The authors also report that deformation monitoring achieved total accuracy between 90.23% and 96.62% for carbon monoxide, ozone, and sulfur dioxide, while nitrogen dioxide had 84.85% accuracy; they do not report run-length results.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors changes in cloud-service performance signatures, which represent relative performance over time. It uses free-trial user observations to identify performance that differs from the existing signature, and treats repeated anomalies as a reason to test for a lasting change. The method uses an event-condition-action framework: an anomaly event prompts a cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart test, and a detected change leads to an update of the signature. The anomaly and event thresholds can be adjusted using feedback from the change-test outcomes. Experiments on constructed performance data found that detection accuracy could reach 95% within a 60-day window, depending on the thresholds.
narrate.key_results: The experiments used 100 simulations, a 360-day provisioning period, 30-day trials, 5 signatures, and 18 consumers; similarity thresholds ranged from 0.1 to 0.9, and anomaly thresholds ranged from 10% to 100%. With the similarity threshold varied, reported average detection delays were 30 to 55 days, and detection accuracy rose from 40% to 95% within the 60-day evaluation window. With the anomaly threshold varied, average delay ranged from 15 to 180 days, while detection accuracy fell from 95% to below 10% as the threshold increased. The authors report that higher similarity thresholds can improve detection accuracy and reduce delay, but increase false positives; higher anomaly thresholds reduce false positives but can sharply reduce detection accuracy.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors restrict the study to one quality-of-service attribute, throughput, for simplicity, and note that the approach could be extended to multiple attributes. narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on live, longer-term service measurements and on varied workloads, providers, and performance attributes, including data with autocorrelation and non-normal distributions. narrate.summary: The paper proposes monitoring a healthcare procedure across its intermediate and final stages, rather than monitoring only its final outcome. narrate.summary: The paper monitors multivariate process measurements for intermittent faults in processes whose observations may be autocorrelated. It proposes an optimally weighted moving average T-squared control chart that weights recent observations using their autocorrelation and cross-correlation, rather than assigning them equal weights. The weighted statistic is compared with a control limit, and the chart signals when the statistic exceeds that limit. The authors also give conditions for when a fault’s appearance and disappearance can be detected and procedures for choosing the weights and window length. Simulations show that the method detected the tested intermittent faults more effectively than the compared charts, including when the process data were autocorrelated.
narrate.key_results: In the numerical example, the significance level was 0.01 and the tested faults had a lower-bound magnitude of 0.42, a minimum active duration of 15 observations, and a minimum inactive duration of 20; the authors found these faults guaranteed detectable with window lengths from 10 to 15. At window length 10, both the proposed chart and the equally weighted chart had a reported FAR of 0.25%, but the proposed chart clearly signaled the faults while the equally weighted chart did not. In the CSTR simulation, with a fault magnitude lower bound of 2.5 K and active and inactive durations of 10 sampling intervals, the proposed chart at window length 10 had a FAR of 0.5%; the equal-weight moving-average Mahalanobis-distance chart had a FAR of 10.25%. For faults with active and inactive durations of one interval, the paper reports a fault detection rate of 53% for window length 10 and 93% for window length 40, with FARs of 0% and 0.25%, respectively; the larger window improved detection but added delay.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors multivariate process measurements for intermittent faults, which may be brief, recurring, and too small to detect reliably from one observation at a time. It proposes moving average Hotelling T-squared control charts using several window lengths at once. Each chart signals when its statistic exceeds its control limit, while results across windows are combined to reject some false alarms, compensate for some missed alarms, and estimate fault start and end times. The paper also derives conditions for when a fault is guaranteed detectable under stated assumptions. Simulations on a two-variable example and a reactor process show that the approach can detect the simulated faults and estimate their time intervals.
narrate.key_results: In the two-variable numerical example, the study used 5,000 training observations, 500 test observations, and a significance level of 0.01; with a stated lower bound of 4 for fault magnitude and 10 sampling intervals for both active and inactive duration, the authors identify window lengths 7 through 10 as guaranteeing detectability. Charts with window lengths 1 and 2 performed poorly in that example, while combining the qualifying windows helped address illustrated false and missed alarms and yielded intervals containing the simulated fault times. In the reactor simulation, the authors used 5,000 fault-free training observations and 400 test observations, sampled at 30 seconds; they report guaranteed detectability for window lengths 5 through 10, whereas lengths 1 and 2 did not guarantee it. The paper reports no run-length or average-run-length results and gives no numerical comparative performance measures across repeated trials.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors video frames from a manufacturing process to detect and locate persistent, spatially clustered high-intensity events, especially overheating hotspots during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). It separates each frame into background, random natural foreground activity, a structured anomaly, and noise. A penalized spatio-temporal model estimates the anomaly, and a sequential likelihood ratio test (LRT) signals when the monitoring statistic exceeds a control limit. The authors evaluate the method with simulated hotspots and real process videos. They report that it detects simulated hotspots much sooner than the benchmark methods and detects all reported hotspot events in the real videos with delays of no more than five frames.
narrate.key_results: In simulations using hotspot sizes of 4, 9, 20, 45, and 80 pixels, the proposed method's reported average run lengths (ARLs) were 3.39, 2.65, 2.29, 2.01, and 1.20 frames, respectively; the methods were calibrated to a false-positive rate of 0.01 using in-control samples. Its reported recall ranged from 0.98 to 0.99, while precision ranged from 0.87 to 0.98 across those sizes. The spatially weighted principal-component benchmark localized the smallest simulated hotspots accurately but had ARLs from 58.39 to 73.19 frames; other benchmarks had weak localization for the smaller simulated hotspots. In three real-video scenarios, the proposed method detected all four reported events in each scenario, with delays of no more than five frames; several benchmark methods missed most events. The reported computation time was 0.015 seconds per sample with the approximation and 0.4 seconds without it, although the real-data methods were tested offline.

narrate.summary: This paper reviews methods for monitoring changes in the covariance matrix of a multivariate process. It organizes the literature by whether the subgroup sample size is at least as large as the number of variables, smaller than the number of variables, whether the mean and covariance are monitored together, or whether the work addresses related topics. The reviewed charts turn covariance information into statistics and signal when those statistics cross control limits. Some methods target increases or decreases in variability, while others monitor broader changes or aim to distinguish covariance changes from mean changes. The authors find that the literature is most developed when subgroup sample size is at least the number of variables, and identify substantial areas needing further work.
narrate.key_results: The review classifies the literature into four categories: covariance monitoring with larger subgroups, covariance monitoring with smaller subgroups, joint monitoring of the mean and covariance, and related topics such as diagnosis and Phase I analysis. It covers Shewhart, cumulative sum (CUSUM), and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) charts, as well as sparse, robust, and nonparametric approaches. Average run length (ARL) is described as a common measure used in the reviewed studies, but the paper does not present a new, unified numerical comparison of chart performance. The authors report that most published work concerns the larger-subgroup setting and identify gaps in comparisons, parameter-estimation effects, non-normal data, and autocorrelated processes.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the literature is uneven: most methods address cases where subgroup sample size is at least the number of variables, while nonparametric covariance charts are concentrated on bivariate processes. They also identify limited work on parameter estimation effects, robust Phase I methods, and monitoring autocorrelated or non-normal processes.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The review does not describe a reproducible literature-search protocol or explicit inclusion criteria, so readers cannot readily assess how complete the surveyed set of papers is. Its performance discussion draws on results from separate studies with differing assumptions and simulation designs, rather than a common benchmark or pooled comparison; the review also provides no new validation on real process data.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for broader comparisons of existing methods, research into misleading signals and adaptive charts, and better guidance for tuning sparse methods. They also recommend more work on diagnosis, parameter estimation, robust Phase I monitoring, high-dimensional and non-normal settings, and autocorrelated data. They identify incorporating process-specific or causal structure as another promising direction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A reproducible search and evidence-synthesis protocol would help future reviews update and verify the coverage of this fast-growing field. Researchers could also establish shared simulation benchmarks and validate leading charts on real process datasets, with practical software and guidance for interpreting a signal and identifying its cause.
