narrate.summary: This review examines charts for monitoring changes in the variability and covariance structure of multiple correlated quality characteristics collected one observation at a time. It organizes the literature into cumulative sum (CUSUM), multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA), Shewhart, nonparametric, and high-dimensional chart families. The methods detect changes in variance, correlation, or both, and most of the reviewed charts assume normally distributed, independent observations. A chart signals when its monitoring statistic crosses its specified control limit or limits. The review finds that many methods exist, but comparatively little research addresses nonparametric, CUSUM, and high-dimensional charts.
narrate.key_results: The authors selected 30 relevant articles published from 1987 to 2019 and classified them into five groups: 4 CUSUM, 14 MEWMA, 6 Shewhart, 2 nonparametric, and 4 high-dimensional articles. Twenty-one articles appeared from 2010 to 2019, including 10 MEWMA articles. The reviewed methods use a range of statistics, including traces, likelihood ratios, norms, spatial signs and ranks, and dissimilarity measures. The authors report that several methods have difficulty detecting decreases in process variances, and that performance depends on the type of shift and chart.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that most reviewed methods assume normality, known process parameters, and independent observations, and that many methods are ineffective at detecting decreases in process variance. They also identify concerns about control limits, limited steady-state evaluation, transient shifts, and the small number of methods for nonparametric and high-dimensional monitoring.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The literature search used Google Scholar, but the review does not provide a fully reproducible search strategy or a detailed account of how screening decisions were made. Its performance comparisons summarize results from different studies with differing assumptions and evaluation settings, rather than applying a common benchmark to all charts.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors recommend developing more charts for high-dimensional data, nonparametric monitoring, and CUSUM monitoring, and extending some Shewhart charts to monitor location and scale together. They also call for work on transient shifts, reliable control limits, steady-state performance, robustness to outliers and non-normality, estimated parameters, and dependent observations.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a reproducible, systematic update of the review that compares selected charts under shared simulation settings, including realistic combinations of variance and correlation changes. Further work could also make implementations readily available and validate chart performance across additional real production processes.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a phase I analysis of wind-turbine power records from supervisory control and data acquisition systems. It estimates the normal power curve from weather variables using multivariate adaptive regression splines, then reduces serial correlation with iterative feasible generalized least squares. A distribution-free recursive segmentation and permutation chart examines the adjusted residuals for changes in their mean, including isolated and step-like changes. The chart uses permutations to assess significance, and the analysts remove detected segments and repeat the analysis until the p-value exceeds a preset threshold. The field examples identified several unusual operating segments, although the authors could not confirm their causes from the available records.
narrate.key_results: The real-data examples used two filtered data sets containing 10,014 and 41,374 points. The power-curve root mean squared errors for the first data set were 39.18 with multivariate adaptive regression splines alone and 30.08 with iterative feasible generalized least squares; for the second, they were 42.86 and 35.84, respectively. The chart analysis used hourly subgroups of 6 observations, allowed up to 50 change points, and used a significance threshold of 0.05. The authors report that removing four detected segments raised the aggregated statistic's p-value to 0.002, and removing four additional segments raised it above 0.05; they interpreted detected patterns as possibly reflecting sensor or transmission problems, down-rating, changing air density, and suboptimal operation.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors multivariate sensor measurements from components in two operating hydropower plants. It trains a self-organizing map (SOM) on data treated as nominal, then uses differences between current and nominal data patterns to detect departures from normal operation. A key performance indicator (KPI) is smoothed over time, and a warning is issued when it falls below a lower control limit (LCL). The method also estimates which sensor variables contribute most to an unusual pattern. In field testing, it detected more than 20 anomalous situations and identified two described cases earlier or with fewer false alarms than the Hotelling chart.
narrate.key_results: The system was tested at two Italian hydropower plants from April 2018 through July 2019, using more than 600 input signals overall; the training data covered May 2017 through March 2018, and the model was retrained every two months during online testing. The authors report more than 20 anomalous situations during 16 months of testing, with severity assessed by plant operators. In one case, a generator temperature sensor warning led to corrective action before further sensor degradation could have stopped a generating unit; estimated avoided costs were EUR 25,000 to EUR 100,000. In another case, the SOM-based KPI signaled a transformer-gas anomaly 20 days before the Hotelling chart did. The comparison was qualitative: the authors report that the Hotelling chart produced several past false positives in one case and did not identify some events well, but provide no numerical detection-rate or run-length measures.

For these three outages, the proposed alternating-current method with limited measurements was faster than the two comparison approaches reported in the paper. narrate.summary: The paper reviews methods for monitoring time-between-events (TBE) data from several processes. It distinguishes data collected as complete vectors, which may not be available until every component has an event, from streams of events occurring at different rates. A chart signals when its monitoring statistic crosses a set threshold, but waiting for complete vectors can delay detection. The authors recommend evaluating such methods with average time-to-signal (ATS), rather than average run length (ARL), because the time between plotted observations varies. In their simulation comparison, the multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) did not consistently detect changes faster than paired univariate exponentially weighted moving average (PEWMA) charts.
narrate.key_results: The simulation comparison used 100,000 replications, four in-control models, and six shift scenarios per model; the control limits were set to give an in-control ATS of 200. The models used baseline scale parameters of 1 and 2 or 10 and 2, with independent data or dependence parameter 0.5; shifts halved or doubled one or both parameters. For the independent model with baseline parameters 1 and 2, halving both gave ATS values of 18.15 for MEWMA and 9.28 for PEWMA, while doubling both gave 24.26 and 23.33. For the dependent model with baseline parameters 1 and 2, halving both gave ATS values of 34.12 for MEWMA and 9.96 for PEWMA; results varied by scenario, and neither approach was uniformly faster.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors wind turbine components using Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) data, including gearbox, generator bearing, and main bearing signals. The method is intended to detect changes in component behavior that may indicate emerging faults. narrate.key_results: Historical validation used data from 2015–2016, covering six wind farms, 150 wind turbines, and 283 megawatts of nominal power; the authors report bearing-failure prediction lead times from 2 weeks to 1–2 months. During the 2017 real-time test, the system delivered 25 anomalous cases: 15 related to gearboxes, 8 to generators, and 2 to main bearings. Operators responded to almost half of the cases, and more than 90% of the cases with operator feedback were reported as true positives.

narrate.summary: The paper evaluates methods for detecting anomalous changes in networks that evolve over time and whose observations are temporally correlated. It monitors network density, maximum node degree, two combinations of those summaries, and a more complex moving-window scan statistic. The summary-statistic charts signal when a value crosses calibrated control limits, while the scan method signals when its statistic exceeds a threshold. Simulations include changes in edge probabilities and changes in expected node degree, using binary and count networks generated from two network models. The main finding is that simple summaries, especially combinations of density and maximum degree, often detect the planted changes as well as or better than the scan statistic.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used 200 simulations per anomaly type, with 100 nodes and 110 time points; the first 50 time points formed the reference period, and the target conditional false alarm probability was 0.03. For a count dynamic latent space model with 33 affected nodes, an odds-ratio change from 1 to 4, and a change lasting 5 time points, the density chart detected 0.980 of anomalies, the maximum-degree and both combination charts detected 1, and the scan statistic detected 0.545. For a binary dynamic degree-corrected stochastic block model with 15 affected nodes and an expected-degree multiplier from 1 to 2.25, the maximum-degree and both combination charts had a detection rate of 1 for the 5-time-point case, compared with 0.085 for density and 0.770 for the scan statistic. Across the degree-change scenarios, density was generally the weakest summary, while the difference statistic often had the strongest area-under-curve performance; the scan statistic was also often weaker than the simpler summaries.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that these summaries will miss anomalies that do not affect them directly, giving as an example two nodes switching from maximum and minimum degree to each other. Their assessment uses simulated network data, and they point out that practical use depends on having enough clean reference-period data to estimate limits; a signal also requires further investigation to identify its cause.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations use networks with 100 nodes and two specified model families, and the planted changes cover selected changes in edge probabilities and expected degree; performance may differ for other network sizes, structures, or anomaly types. The comparison reports detection rate and area under the curve rather than detection delay or run length, and it does not validate the calibrated limits on real network processes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the univariate monitoring approach to multivariate monitoring of density, maximum degree, and their combinations, including accounting for covariance when calibrating joint control limits.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test these charts on real network streams and examine how reference-period length, contamination, and estimation uncertainty affect false alarms and detection. They could also add methods to locate affected nodes after a signal and assess performance for network sizes, dependence patterns, and anomaly types beyond those simulated here.

narrate.summary: The paper develops sequential tests for detecting a change in the distribution of a finite sequence of observations, including sequences with dependence. It chooses a monitoring statistic and a changing control limit to optimize a selected measure of detection delay while meeting a false-alarm constraint. The chart signals when its statistic reaches or exceeds the dynamic control limit. The authors show that different delay measures lead to different optimal tests, and give a way to calculate their minimum generalized out-of-control average run length. Simulations illustrate better detection performance than selected standard charts at comparable in-control average run lengths.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves optimality for its constructed test for each specified delay measure and finite horizon, under its likelihood-ratio assumptions. In 60 independent normal observations with a shift from mean 0 to mean 1 and in-control average run length near 40, the proposed tests had generalized out-of-control average run lengths of 139.18 and 49.26 for the two respective measures; the corresponding CUSUM values were 148.07 and 54.44. In the 60-observation Markov example, where the correlation parameter changed from 0.5 to 0.1, at in-control average run length near 40, the proposed tests reported values of 409.76 and 57.86, compared with 474.64 and 59.71 for CUSUM. In a separate mean-shift example from 0 to 0.2 with in-control average run length about 40, a dynamic-limit CUSUM had Lorden delay 22.951 versus 23.425 for constant-limit CUSUM; in the exponential example with in-control average run length about 2, a dynamic-limit Shiryaev–Roberts test had Pollak delay 1.2743 versus 1.3165 for its constant-limit version.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors healthcare claims data aggregated into time series for costs, utilization, patient counts, and other measures across clinical and demographic groupings. narrate.summary: The paper monitors a univariate stream with serial dependence for permanent changes in its mean, or level shifts. It models the process and uses one-step prediction errors to assess possible shift times within a moving window. The chart takes the largest absolute standardized test statistic across that window and signals when it reaches or exceeds a calibrated critical value. The authors calibrate that value by simulation to achieve a chosen in-control false-alarm rate. In simulations of first-order autoregressive processes, the method performed comparably to a cumulative sum chart when both were tuned well, and was more reliable at locating the change point.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used first-order autoregressive processes with coefficients from -0.95 to 0.95, innovation standard deviation 1, and 20,000 repetitions; shift-size parameter values ranged from 0 to 2.0, with examples at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5. Critical values were calibrated to an in-control average run length (ARL0) of 370.4, with a reported 95% confidence interval of 365.5 to 375.4, and window widths up to 100. The authors report that their method was 39% better overall than the first cumulative sum (CUSUM) setting and comparable to the second setting; for shift sizes below 1, CUSUM could have an out-of-control average run length (ARL1) up to 33% lower, while for shift sizes above 1 the proposed method generally performed better, reaching up to 48 times better performance for large positive autoregressive coefficients. The proposed chart’s probability of signaling within 10 time steps of the true change point increased with the window horizon, while CUSUM’s change-point detection was more sensitive to its tuning parameter.

narrate.summary: This paper presents a method for monitoring manufactured parts from three-dimensional surface scans, including meshes with different numbers of points and no point-to-point registration. For each part, it estimates the spectrum of the Laplace-Beltrami operator and monitors the lower eigenvalues as a summary of the part’s geometry and size. The online distribution-free multivariate exponentially weighted moving average chart uses weighted ranks and signals when its statistic crosses a permutation-based, time-varying limit. A separate Phase I method is proposed for startup, and an Iterated Closest Point procedure can help locate a defect after an alarm. In simulations, the spectral method detected global shape changes quickly, while small localized defects were harder to detect unless the meshes were dense.
narrate.key_results: For the online chart, 100 reference parts, the first 15 eigenvalues, a weighting parameter of 0.01, and a false alarm probability of 0.005 gave a nominal in-control average run length of 200. In simulations of barrel-shaped cylinders with about 2,000 mesh points and isotropic noise with standard deviation 0.05, the average run length was 10.7949 for shift magnitude 0.0005 and 2.0336 for shift magnitude 0.005. For localized defects on smaller meshes, the spectral chart’s average run length was 158.1168 for chipped defect 1, 91.3750 for chipped defect 2, and 3.6450 for a protrusion; after mesh preprocessing to about 5,000 points, these values improved to 5.0943, 4.4362, and 2.4341. In the Phase I simulations, the false alarm probabilities were close to the nominal 0.05, and for cylinder shift magnitude 0.005 the alarm probability was 1.0 when using eigenvalues 2 through 75, compared with 0.0741 when using eigenvalues 2 through 100.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on surface meshes of genus 0 and note that extending their work to volumetric data remains future work. narrate.summary: The paper monitors a sequence of independent observations for a persistent change in location, expressed as a shift away from a known median in a continuous symmetric distribution. Its proposed signed sequential rank Shiryaev-Roberts scheme uses the sign and sequential rank of each observation, so its in-control behavior does not depend on the distribution’s shape, scale, or moments. The chart signals when its accumulating statistic reaches or exceeds a control limit selected for a target in-control average run length. Simulations compare it with a signed sequential rank cumulative sum chart and an earlier nonparametric Shiryaev-Roberts scheme. The authors find that the proposed chart is broadly effective and often detects small shifts more quickly than the rank-based cumulative sum chart, while also illustrating it on coal-ash laboratory differences.
narrate.key_results: For an in-control average run length of 500, the authors provide Wilcoxon signed sequential rank Shiryaev-Roberts control limits across reference values from 0.05 to 1.00; for example, the limit is 6.05 at reference value 0.15. In simulations with a Laplace in-control distribution, a change point at observation 100, and an in-control average run length of 500, the proposed chart’s conditional average delay was 44 observations for an actual shift of 0.25 with reference value 0.12, compared with 45 for a normal Shiryaev-Roberts chart using the paper’s adjusted-shift approximation. The authors report that the proposed chart and the nonparametric Shiryaev-Roberts comparator often have lower delays than the rank-based cumulative sum chart for shifts well below the target, while the comparator’s performance is less robust when tuning assumes the wrong distribution. In the coal-ash example, the cumulative sum chart signaled at observation 91, and the proposed chart and the nonparametric comparator signaled at observation 93; the estimated change points were 77 and 78 for the cumulative sum and proposed charts, respectively.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on location changes in symmetric distributions with a known median and identify detecting scale changes or location and scale changes in asymmetric distributions as matters for further research. They also note that their normal-chart approximation can be poor when the shift is large and the change occurs at the outset, and that generating accurate NPSR control limits at nominal in-control average run lengths of 1,000 or more is computationally impractical across a wide range of reference values.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method assumes independent observations from a continuous symmetric in-control distribution with a known median; the paper does not evaluate how dependence or an uncertain median affects false alarms. Although the ranks remove the need to specify the in-control distribution for calibration, choosing the reference value still depends on the expected shift and may use an estimated distribution-specific quantity from Phase I data. The simulation comparisons cover a limited set of distributions and competitors, and the real-data illustration is a single coal-ash example rather than a broader validation across operational processes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating signed sequential rank Shiryaev-Roberts schemes for detecting scale changes. They also propose developing schemes for detecting location and scale changes in asymmetric distributions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the chart’s false-alarm and delay properties when observations are autocorrelated or when the median and tuning quantities must be estimated, including the effects of estimation uncertainty. Further work could test the method on more operational data and assess procedures for diagnosing the direction and timing of a change after a signal, including the proposed change-point estimator.

narrate.summary: The paper compares charts for monitoring changes in the variability of correlated quality characteristics, using either individual observations or groups of observations. It evaluates a smoothed individual-observation chart and charts based on fixed or moving groups, including statistics formed from covariance estimates. A chart signals when its monitoring statistic crosses an upper or lower control limit; the authors calibrate the charts to an in-control average time to signal of 370. Across the simulated conditions, individual-observation monitoring is generally quickest, especially for increases in variability, while moving-group charts perform well for decreases. The authors recommend individual observations when possible and overlapping groups when subgroup monitoring is required.
narrate.key_results: The simulation used 50,000 runs for processes with 2 or 10 variables and calibrated in-control ATS to 370. For 10 variables, no correlation shift, and a variance multiplier of 2, the MEWMS chart with smoothing constant 0.2 had an ATS of 4, compared with 7 for the OTCC and 15 for the NTCC. For a variance multiplier of 0.6 in the same setting, the OTCC had an ATS of 10, while the MEWMS chart with smoothing constant 0.2 had an ATS of 18. In the illustrative case study, the data were generated with 50 in-control observations, 30 observations at a variance multiplier of 2.5, and 20 at 0.5; the authors report quickest detection after 7 observations for the increase and 15 for the decrease. They also found that overlapping charts generally outperformed non-overlapping charts and that larger subgroups often reduced performance, particularly for large shifts.

narrate.summary: This paper presents a simulation framework for comparing methods that monitor dynamic networks for changes. It compares charts based on global network summaries, a moving-window scan, and methods that monitor estimated network-model parameters. The changes studied include increases in communication, changes in node connection propensities, and changes in community structure. A method signals when its monitored statistic crosses its control limit or meets its scan threshold. Across the simulated settings, no method performs best for every type of change, so the appropriate method depends on the change of interest.
narrate.key_results: The authors compared 15 methods using 1,000 simulation runs per setting, with 200 in-control networks followed by up to 50 changed networks. With no change and network dependence set to 0.5, false detection rates rose to roughly 20% to 50% for many methods; this was not seen to the same extent for independent networks, where the dependence setting was 1. For a global increase in communication in a one-community network, most methods detected the change in nearly 100% of runs, and methods 1, 3, 7, 9, and 14 had average conditional expected delays below 10 observations. For a local increase affecting one-fifth of the nodes, method 1 detected more than 60% of changes with 40 nodes and more than 90% with 100 nodes, while the other methods generally had weaker detection. Method 15 performed best for node-propensity changes, while method 14 was strong across many two-community changes; the authors recommend combining these two methods as a broader strategy.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors high-dimensional data streams whose variables have a sparse correlation structure and may contain outliers. It proposes robust sparse probabilistic principal component analysis, which reduces the data to interpretable latent features using Bayesian variational inference and Laplacian priors. The method detects changes either in the latent features or in residual noise that does not fit the learned structure. A signal occurs when either monitoring statistic exceeds its chi-square cutoff. Simulations and an in-line Raman spectroscopy case study found shorter detection delays than the comparison methods in the tested settings.
narrate.key_results: In loading-recovery simulations with 500 observed variables, the average subspace deviation for RSPCA at sample size 100 and outlier proportion 0.2 was 0.40, compared with 0.42 for ROSPCA and 0.51 for SRPCA; at sample size 500, the corresponding values were 0.16, 0.17, and 0.18. In monitoring simulations, the authors trained on 500 in-control observations, tested latent-variable mean shifts from 0 to 2 standard deviations, used outlier proportions of 0.1 and 0.2, and set the in-control ARL to 200; RSPCA had the lowest plotted detection delay among the four methods. For the Raman case study, mean detection delays for the three defects were 4.1, 3.2, and 2.5 observations with RSPCA, with reported standard deviations of 3.4, 3.4, and 1.6. The corresponding delays were 25.6, 17.2, and 19.7 for classical PCA; 20.1, 18.9, and 10.6 for sparse PCA; and 12.1, 16, and 9.6 for robust PCA.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a cost-optimal control chart for monitoring a single patient characteristic over time, and demonstrates it with low-density lipoprotein levels in patients at cardiovascular risk. Its Markov-chain model allows shifts to vary in size, treatment to be imperfect, and planned visits to be missed. At a visit, the chart signals when the measured level exceeds a selected critical increase above the target, prompting treatment. The authors estimate long-run cost from the stationary distribution of a discretized Markov chain and can optimize expected cost alone or combine it with cost variability. In the healthcare example, the selected monitoring interval and critical increase differed from usual medical practice, and including cost variability reduced it with only a small increase in expected cost.
narrate.key_results: When optimizing expected cost alone for the Hungarian low-density lipoprotein example, the selected interval was 56.57 days and the critical increase was 0.143 millimoles per liter; the resulting average daily cost was EUR 0.469 and its standard deviation was EUR 0.562. With 10% weight assigned to cost standard deviation, the selected interval was 64.76 days and the critical increase was 0.129 millimoles per liter; average daily cost was EUR 0.477 and its standard deviation was EUR 0.418. In a simulation with weight 0.9, process standard deviation 1, shift rate 0.2, and expected shift size 2, the theoretical average cost was 37.75 and cost standard deviation was 150.33; the baseline simulation estimates were 36.51 and 199.37, respectively. The paper reports no run-length or detection-time results, and found no major change from the two sensitizing rules it tested.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors a project's duration-based schedule performance and cost performance over time. It uses Earned Duration Management indices, then adjusts their measurements for non-normality and autocorrelation before charting the model residuals. A point outside the chart limits signals an unusual change that managers should investigate; points within the limits are treated as acceptable variation. In a construction project observed weekly for 42 weeks, the charts identified schedule exceptions in weeks 3 and 9 and a cost exception in week 3. The authors conclude that charts used alongside the original index values can help project teams detect problems sooner.
narrate.key_results: The case study used 42 weekly observations; at a significance level of 0.20, the Earned Duration Index was treated as normally distributed with a p-value of 0.222, while the Duration Performance Index and Cost Performance Index had p-values of 0.036 and 0.026 and were transformed. The selected Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average models were (4,1,1) for the Cost Performance Index, (1,1,1) for the Duration Performance Index, and (4,1,1) for the Earned Duration Index. The charts signaled an unusually poor schedule result for the Duration Performance Index in week 3 and the Earned Duration Index in week 9; the cost chart signaled an unusually high Cost Performance Index in week 3. The reported upper and lower limits were 1.792 and -2.008 for the Duration Performance Index, 0.1421 and -0.1428 for the Earned Duration Index, and 1.158 and -1.159 for the Cost Performance Index.

narrate.summary: The paper presents nonparametric methods for monitoring sequences of measurements, including individual observations, batches, and multivariate data. It converts observations to sequential normal scores by ranking each new observation against earlier observations and mapping the rank to a normal score. Shewhart-type charts signal when a score or summary statistic crosses a control limit, while cumulative sum and exponentially weighted moving average charts accumulate evidence of persistent changes; squared scores are also used to detect increases in spread. Examples show that these methods can detect changes in location, scale, or both, and can estimate when a change began, without requiring a specified distribution for the original measurements.
narrate.key_results: The paper provides worked examples rather than a broad simulation study with systematic run-length comparisons. For batches of five in a location-change example calibrated to an average run length of 500, the cumulative sum chart signaled at batch 22, compared with batch 23 for a cited competing method; the exponentially weighted moving average example signaled at batch 23. For a scale-change example with a target average run length of 200, the exponentially weighted moving average of squared scores signaled at observation 29 and estimated the change point as observation 19, while the generated change occurred at observation 21. In a multivariate example with a change at observation 11, the proposed method signaled at observation 20 for location-only and combined changes, and at observation 20 for a scale-only change; the authors also report an example where an exponentially weighted moving average signaled at observation 24 with a target average run length of 200.

They say that the properties of the proposed multivariate method need further study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper’s evidence is largely illustrative and relies on a small set of examples, including generated data and examples adapted from other sources, rather than extensive evaluations across many shift sizes and underlying distributions. The method assumes independent observations or batches, and the paper does not assess performance under serial correlation; in multivariate examples, estimated correlations from relatively small reference samples may also make limits and detection performance unstable. The comparisons cover selected nonparametric and parametric procedures, not a comprehensive set of modern competing charts.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for further study of the proposed methods’ properties. They also suggest comparing the squared-score method’s power with methods that combine location and scale statistics, and note that a nonparametric version of the cumulative-sum-on-Hotelling-statistic approach may help detect subtler changes.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate false alarm rates and detection delays through large, reproducible simulations across different distributions, shift patterns, batch sizes, and serial dependence conditions. narrate.summary: The paper studies monitoring the process mean when measurements may contain outliers or come from a contaminated distribution. It builds an adaptive robust chart by applying changing zone-based limits to a cumulative sum chart that uses sample medians. The chart signals when its cumulative-sum statistic crosses the applicable control limit; repeated values on the same side of the center cause that side's limit to move inward. The authors compare the method with average run length (ARL) simulations for normal and contaminated observations. They report that the adaptive median-based chart performs well relative to the other charts for many shifts in the contaminated-data comparison.
narrate.key_results: The study simulated 10,000 runs with subgroup size 5 and shifts of 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, and 1.5. The contaminated observations were a mixture of 94% from a normal distribution with variance 1 and 6% from one with variance 6.25; at shift 0.0, the adaptive median-based chart had an ARL of 466.2, compared with 430.0 for the non-adaptive median-based cumulative sum chart. In the paper's normalized relative-ARL table for contaminated data, the adaptive chart had values of 130.3 at shift 0.1, 25.9 at 0.3, 12.7 at 0.5, 8.47 at 0.7, and 5.79 at 1.0, lower than the other listed charts at those shifts. At shift 1.5, its value was 3.97, slightly higher than the median-based exponentially weighted moving average chart's 3.93; the authors nevertheless describe the adaptive chart as the best choice for contaminated data overall.

narrate.summary: The paper studies standard-deviation charts for monitoring process variability when Phase I data may contain outliers or contamination. It compares conventional estimates with robust scale estimates, paired with conventional or robust location estimates of the subgroup scales. A Phase II sample signals when its estimated scale falls outside the lower or upper control limits established from Phase I. The authors evaluate false signals and detection delay using average run length (ARL) in simulations of diffuse symmetric, diffuse asymmetric, and localized contamination. They find that robust estimates generally improve monitoring under diffuse contamination, while the conventional sample standard deviation paired with a robust location estimate performs well for localized contamination.
narrate.key_results: For the in-control target of 370.4, conventional methods under diffuse symmetric contamination had an ARL of 305.6 at the reported low contamination level and 78.1 at the high level. For the same contamination model at a Phase II standard-deviation multiplier of 1.4, the conventional standard deviation and mean combination had an ARL of 480.9 at the highest contamination level, compared with 287.5 for the logistic M scale estimator paired with Harrell-Davis. Under diffuse asymmetric contamination at the highest reported contamination level, conventional methods signaled falsely on average every 38.5 samples, while the Q estimator had an in-control ARL of 364; the authors also identify this estimator as having strong detection performance for this model. Under localized contamination, conventional methods had an in-control ARL that fell from 335.6 at low contamination to 88.2 at high contamination, while the sample standard deviation paired with the Harrell-Davis location estimate achieved an out-of-control ARL of 66.2 at a Phase II standard-deviation multiplier of 1.4.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors sequential multivariate observations for a covariance change in which a low-rank signal subspace emerges from a noisy background. It proposes a largest-eigenvalue Shewhart chart and a Subspace-CUSUM procedure, which estimates the emerging subspace while accumulating evidence. The Shewhart chart signals when the largest eigenvalue of a sliding-window covariance matrix reaches a threshold; the Subspace-CUSUM signals when its accumulated statistic reaches a threshold. The authors derive approximations for the average run length (ARL) of the Shewhart chart and a lower bound for its expected detection delay (EDD), and give guidance for choosing the Subspace-CUSUM drift. Simulations and examples involving human gestures and seismic signals illustrate the methods; the simulation comparison finds that the better of the two proposed charts depends on signal strength.
narrate.key_results: For dimension 10 and window length 200, the threshold approximation accounting for overlapping windows was closer to simulated thresholds than the approximation that ignored temporal correlation: for target ARLs from 5,000 to 50,000, the reported threshold divided by window length ranged from 1.699 to 1.744 with the correlation adjustment, versus 1.738 to 1.816 without it. In simulations with dimension 5, noise variance 1, and window length 50, Subspace-CUSUM had lower EDD than the largest-eigenvalue chart at signal strengths 0.5 and 1, while the largest-eigenvalue chart did better at strength 1.5; the exact CUSUM with known parameters was the best-performing baseline. In the seismic example, the methods identified events at 615, 2,127, and 6,371 seconds, compared with catalog times of 594, 2,124, and 6,369 seconds, and the authors report that all detection delays were within 20 seconds. The paper also demonstrates gesture-change detection on a 54-attribute sensor dataset, with the Subspace-CUSUM statistic rising at the indicated change point for both rank-one and rank-10 pre-change subspace estimates.

narrate.limitations_stated: The main formulation assumes independent Gaussian observations and known noise variance, and the analysis focuses on a rank-one spiked covariance change. The authors state that projecting data to reduce the switching-subspace problem loses information, and that the sequential largest-eigenvalue procedure does not inherit the optimality of the related offline test. Their Subspace-CUSUM calibration and eigenvector approximation rely on a sufficiently large window; the paper describes its ARL shortcut for that procedure as relying on a weak-dependence argument.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The methods may be sensitive to departures from the assumed independent Gaussian model, including autocorrelation, heavy tails, or changing noise variance, none of which are evaluated in the reported simulations. The empirical comparisons are limited: the simulations use a narrow set of dimensions, window sizes, and signal strengths, while real-data comparisons focus mainly on Hotelling’s chart rather than a broad set of covariance-monitoring competitors; the seismic thresholds are calibrated using an initial 600 seconds of data.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify proving that Subspace-CUSUM is first-order asymptotically optimal as a goal for future work. They also say the rank-one results can be generalized to higher rank using similar ideas, but do not present that analysis here.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the procedures under autocorrelated, non-Gaussian data and unknown or time-varying noise, and develop calibration that remains reliable when the window is not large relative to dimension. It could also evaluate more covariance-chart competitors, provide methods to diagnose the estimated changed subspace after a signal, and validate performance across additional operational processes.

narrate.summary: The paper presents dictionary learning (DL) for robust online classification of manual material handling (MMH) activities from wearable-sensor measurements. Its DL-based robust online classification (DL-ROC) method learns smaller, class-specific dictionaries while reducing redundancy within classes and similarity between classes. A hybrid error measure is intended to make the method less sensitive to outliers and non-Gaussian noise. For each new sample, the method assigns the class with the greatest share of estimated sparse-representation energy; it does not signal a process change using a control chart. In a laboratory study of eight simulated MMH activities, the method achieved a mean F-score of 0.9611 and a reported classification time of 0.0037 seconds per sample.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used wearable-sensor data from 10 volunteers and eight simulated MMH activity classes; training participants and test participants were separated, with seven used for training and three for testing, and the classification experiment was repeated for 100 runs. The proposed method's mean F-score was 0.9611, compared with 0.8821 for sparse representation classification using the greedy hybrid norm method and 0.8661 using orthogonal matching pursuit. Its reported time was 0.0037 seconds per sample, compared with 0.0056 seconds for the greedy hybrid norm method and 0.0019 seconds for orthogonal matching pursuit. These are classification results, not run-length or shift-detection results; the paper reports no in-control setting or process shifts.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors the quality of vital-sign measurements collected by telehealth devices at elder care centers, where daily data can be incomplete. It adapts a multivariate Hotelling T-squared chart to account for missing measurements by charting daily averages and adjusting their covariance for the available participant overlap. The chart signals when its statistic exceeds a simulated upper control limit, indicating a possible change in the measurement system or in participants’ vital signs. Retrospective and prospective case studies show that the method detected known measurement problems, including capped blood-pressure readings, and was implemented for real-time monitoring.
narrate.key_results: The authors set the false alarm rate to 0.02, corresponding to an average of one false alarm every 50 days, and obtained simulated upper control limits of 17.31 for center A and 18.59 for center B. In center A, where systolic blood pressure readings were capped at 136, the chart signaled the problem beginning on February 20, four days after the issue began. In prospective monitoring at center B, a signal after one week led to discovery of diastolic blood pressure readings capped on March 9, and the device was adjusted. Later signals were attributed to one participant’s high heart rate and to an unusual combination of high systolic blood pressure and low oxygen saturation.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method assumes that missingness is at random and that the daily average vectors are approximately independent and multivariate normal. narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from only two centers, with 24 participants in center A and 12 in center B, so it gives limited evidence about performance across other populations, devices, or patterns of missingness. Averaging across participants may conceal an individual’s health change, while a real clinical change can also trigger a signal that is intended to identify a measurement-system problem. Parameter estimates rely on an initial reference period of 19 days, making results potentially sensitive to the stability and representativeness of that short period.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose comparing the method with existing approaches for missing observations, including imputation methods. They also identify a multivariate cumulative sum chart with dynamic probability control limits as a possible extension and call for research on robust covariance estimation that can handle outliers, missingness, and slight departures from normality in grouped data.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test detection and false-alarm behavior across controlled shifts, different missing-data mechanisms, and a wider range of participant counts, including cases where the missingness assumption is not met. Field validation across more centers and devices, along with procedures to distinguish measurement faults from genuine health changes and to identify affected participants after a signal, would help establish practical use.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how the Multivariate Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (MEWMA) statistic behaves after it has run for a long time, and how that behavior affects detection delays for changes in the process mean. The chart signals when the squared distance of its statistic from the in-control mean exceeds a threshold. The author derives steady-state densities and uses integral equations with numerical quadrature to calculate conditional, cyclical, and worst-case average run lengths (ARLs). A key result is that the multivariate steady-state density can be separated into distance and direction components, making the calculations more feasible. The calculations show that steady-state performance can differ from zero-state performance, especially as the data dimension increases, and that MEWMA can detect many shifts more quickly than a Hotelling chart.
narrate.key_results: With smoothing constant 0.1 and an in-control ARL set to 200, the conditional steady-state ARL at a mean-shift magnitude of 1 was 9.68 for dimension 2, 11.36 for dimension 4, and 14.47 for dimension 10; the corresponding cyclical values were 9.69, 11.38, and 14.51. For the in-control case under the same settings, conditional steady-state ARLs were 192.6 for dimension 2 and 189.6 for dimension 10, compared with the target zero-state value of 200. Results from the new numerical method matched the reported Monte Carlo estimates to the displayed precision, using one billion replications for the simulation checks; the method used 30 quadrature nodes, versus Markov-chain matrices with dimensions from 1,500 to 6,000 in the cited comparison. For a shift magnitude of 1 and in-control ARL of 200, the smoothing constants that minimized conditional steady-state ARL were 0.136, 0.114, and 0.089 for dimensions 2, 4, and 10, respectively.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. They describe the uniform distribution of the statistic’s direction on the unit sphere as a heuristic conjecture in motivating the steady-state density decomposition.

narrate.future_work_stated: The author proposes using the density decomposition to calculate detection delays at successive change times, then examining how those delays converge to the steady-state ARL. This would help assess how well the steady-state measure represents performance.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method under estimated process parameters, autocorrelation, non-normal data, and changes in covariance as well as mean. narrate.summary: The beta regression control chart (BRCC) monitors continuous fractions and proportions that lie between zero and one and may depend on control variables. It models both the expected value and the dispersion of the monitored variable using beta regression. For each observation, the chart calculates limits from the fitted beta distribution for its control-variable values. A point outside those limits signals that the process may be out of control. The authors report faster detection of changes than the comparison charts in simulations, and illustrate the method with tire-manufacturing and relative-humidity data.
narrate.key_results: The Monte Carlo study used 50,000 replications and set the in-control average run length (ARL) to 200; although sample sizes of 200, 300, 500, and 1,000 were studied, the paper presents results for 200 and 1,000. Mean shifts ranged from -0.15 to 0.15 in increments of 0.01, and dispersion shifts ranged from 0.00 to 0.15 in increments of 0.01; with the in-control ARL fixed at 200, the variable-dispersion beta chart generally had lower out-of-control ARL than the constant-dispersion beta chart and the normal regression chart. The six simulation scenarios covered mean values around 0.40 with dispersion values around 0.156, 0.099, and 0.070, and mean values around 0.20, 0.80, and 0.08 with dispersion around 0.070. In the tire example, using an in-control ARL of 200, the BRCC signaled observation six; in the 729-observation humidity example, it identified five atypical observations, while the other charts identified fewer or none.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes charts for monitoring the mean and standard deviation of a normally distributed process when measurements below a fixed detection threshold are left censored. It estimates the in-control process parameters iteratively and replaces each censored value with its conditional expected value. The method charts subgroup averages and standard deviations of the resulting values, using upper control limits to signal increases in the mean or dispersion. The limits are obtained by simulation for several subgroup sizes and censoring proportions. In a geotextile flow-capacity example with substantial censoring, neither chart signals an out-of-control condition.
narrate.key_results: The authors simulated more than 1,000 estimates for each censoring level to construct limits, targeting a Type I error probability of 0.0027; the reported subgroup sizes are 3, 5, 10, and 20. In the geotextile example, 100 reference subgroups of size 5 were used, with a censoring threshold of 50 ml per hour and an estimated theoretical censoring proportion of 0.843. The estimated in-control mean was 49.0279 and the estimated standard deviation was 0.9915; the reported upper limits were 50.43583 for subgroup averages and 2.0524 for subgroup standard deviations. No plotted subgroup in the example exceeded either limit, but the paper does not report run-length or shifted-process detection results.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that severe censoring can produce substantially different or biased parameter estimates and leaves little information in each subgroup for detecting changes. They also note that iterative maximum-likelihood estimation can require substantial computation when censoring is high, and that decreases in the mean or dispersion can be difficult to detect in relevant censoring conditions.

It signals when the largest component exceeds a simulated control limit, and the component that signals also indicates the likely change type. narrate.key_results: The authors calibrated limits by simulation for in-control average run length (ARL) targets of 200, 370, 500, and 1,000, using 10,000 replications. narrate.summary: The paper monitors streams of attributed networks, where edges represent relationships between nodes and may be binary or weighted. A generalized linear model (GLM) represents edge formation using node or edge attributes, while a state-transition model captures gradual changes in the network over time. An extended Kalman filter (EKF) updates the model parameters sequentially, and the method calculates Pearson residuals by comparing each incoming network with its one-step-ahead prediction. An exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart signals when the average residual crosses a control limit, indicating an abrupt change beyond the modeled dynamics. Simulations show faster detection of smaller shifts than the two benchmark methods, and the Enron example signals around the period of the company scandal.
narrate.key_results: The authors calibrated the charts to an in-control average run length of 200 using Monte Carlo simulation. For a global change in a binary network with shift size delta equal to 1.5, the dynamic method had an out-of-control average run length of 8.57, compared with 113.27 for the static method and 59.32 for the sliding-window method; the corresponding reported standard errors were 0.144, 3.869, and 2.770. The authors report that for shifts smaller than 2.5, the dynamic method detected changes faster than both benchmarks across the simulated cases; local changes in binary networks were difficult for all three methods to detect. In the Enron email example, the chart signaled between weeks 79 and 89, and a CEO-to-CEO analysis identified communication changes around weeks 76 and 89.

key_equations.name: State transition model
key_equations.explanation: The parameter vector beta at time t depends on the transition matrix F, the previous parameter vector, the constant vector xi, and the random state error epsilon at time t.

key_equations.name: Pearson residual
key_equations.explanation: The residual r for edge i at time t plus one is the observed edge value w minus its one-step-ahead prediction, divided by the square root of the prediction variance.

key_equations.name: EWMA statistic
key_equations.explanation: The statistic z at time t plus one combines the current average Pearson residual r-bar with the previous statistic z, using weight lambda for the current residual.

key_equations.name: EWMA control limits
key_equations.explanation: The upper and lower limits at time t are plus and minus the product of multiplier l, in-control residual standard deviation s, and the square-root term determined by lambda and t.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that local changes in binary networks are difficult to detect because the available data may not capture the excessive communications underlying the change. narrate.summary: The paper proposes a Shewhart-type chart for monitoring the mean of a normally distributed process using neoteric ranked set sampling (NRSS). For each sampling cycle, the method ranks one set of k squared units using an inexpensive ordering criterion, then measures k units chosen at specified ranks. The chart plots the sample mean and signals when it falls below the lower control limit or above the upper control limit. The authors compare its detection performance with simple random sampling (SRS) and other ranked-set approaches using simulations, including scenarios with imperfect ranking. In the simulated settings, NRSS generally detects mean shifts faster, and an illustration using concrete-strength data shows the same pattern for the imposed shift.
narrate.key_results: Under perfect ranking, the in-control average run length (ARL) was about 370.5, and the NRSS chart had lower out-of-control ARLs than SRS, RSS, ERSS, and MRSS in the reported comparisons. For a shift of 0.8 standard-error units with sample size 3, the ARL was 21.25 for NRSS and 71.55 for SRS; with sample size 5 and a shift of 1.6 units, the reported values were 1.46 and 12.38, respectively. Across the imperfect-ranking simulations, NRSS had lower ARLs than SRS in 147 of 150 nonzero-shift scenarios, while performance generally worsened as the correlation between the ranked auxiliary measure and the process variable decreased. In the concrete-strength illustration with sample size 3 and an imposed shift of 1.2 units, the NRSS chart had 13 points beyond its limits, compared with 6 for RSS and 2 for SRS.

key_equations.name: NRSS sample mean
key_equations.explanation: The NRSS sample mean is formed from n cycles and k selected observations per cycle; i indexes selected ranks, j indexes cycles, and each Y is the observation selected at the indicated rank.

key_equations.name: Variance of the NRSS sample mean
key_equations.explanation: The variance depends on the variances of the k selected ranked observations and their pairwise covariances; n is the number of cycles, k is the sample size per cycle, and i and i' index selected ranks.

key_equations.name: NRSS control limits
key_equations.explanation: The lower control limit, center line, and upper control limit use the in-control mean mu-zero, the amplitude parameter A, and the standard deviation of the NRSS sample mean.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that NRSS requires ranking k squared units together in one set, which may be operationally difficult when ranking relies on visual judgment. They also report that chart efficiency declines when ranking is imperfect and the correlation between the auxiliary measure and the variable of interest is lower.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations cover normally distributed processes, sample sizes of 3, 4, and 5, and a limited set of shift and correlation values; they do not assess autocorrelated or non-normal process data. The concrete-strength example uses observations as a reference population and introduces an artificial shift, so it does not validate the chart in prospective monitoring of an actual manufacturing process. Although the method allows reference-sample estimates, the paper does not broadly assess how estimation uncertainty affects long-run performance across operating conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest developing NRSS designs based on two or more ordering cycles. They also note that such extensions could be compared with existing double ranked-set methods, while recognizing their greater operational effort.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the chart under non-normality, autocorrelation, and changing or weak auxiliary-variable relationships, and quantify the effects of estimating in-control parameters from limited reference samples. Prospective validation on real manufacturing streams, methods to investigate causes after a signal, and accessible software for constructing the chart would also help assess practical use.

narrate.summary: The paper examines how to economically design charts that monitor process means, with numerical studies of univariate exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) and multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) charts. These charts accumulate information from earlier samples, so their run-length behavior depends on the history of the chart statistic. The paper shows that the Lorenzen–Vance cost formula, which relies on average run lengths, does not correctly account for this memory. A chart signals when its accumulated statistic crosses the upper control limit. In the tested settings, using the original formula could produce substantially higher costs than simulation-based economic design.
narrate.key_results: The study compared the methods on 36 benchmark instances, using 18 process scenarios for each of the EWMA and MEWMA cases. Across these instances, the original formula's estimated costs differed from simulation results by as much as 20%; the discrepancies generally grew as the smoothing weight decreased. Choosing chart parameters using the original formula instead of simulation increased cost by 0.20% to 45.64% for EWMA and by 0.26% to 44.55% for MEWMA. For the non-memory case, where the smoothing weight was 1, the maximum difference between the original formula and simulation was 0.35%. The corrected formula was close to simulation on five selected MEWMA instances, but the authors found it computationally unhelpful.

key_equations.name: MEWMA chart signal
key_equations.explanation: The chart signals at sample m when statistic Y sub m, formed from EWMA state Z sub m and its covariance matrix Sigma of Z sub m, exceeds the upper control limit UL.

key_equations.name: Simulation estimate of long-run average cost
key_equations.explanation: The estimated cost F is the sum of the costs C sub i divided by the sum of durations T sub i across N simulated quality-control cycles.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their corrected formula is not an efficient computational method because its required quantities must themselves be estimated, for example by time-consuming simulation. They also say that earlier studies using the original formula require reappraisal.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison covers equal-weight EWMA and MEWMA charts and a finite set of 36 constructed benchmark instances; it does not numerically validate the claimed problem for CUSUM or Bayesian charts. The study assumes a normal process model with specified parameters and uses simulated rather than real process data, so it does not establish how parameter estimation, autocorrelation, non-normality, or operational conditions affect the economic-design errors.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose reappraising published economic-design results that relied on the original formula, using the simulation method in this paper. They also identify developing a more computationally efficient method as an open research direction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the economic impact of parameter estimation, autocorrelation, and non-normal process data, and evaluate the approach on real manufacturing processes. They could also extend the numerical comparisons to CUSUM and Bayesian charts and provide a maintained, reproducible software implementation.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors six database management system (DBMS) statistics, collected once per minute, to help identify disorder periods and related events. Its method treats changes that are difficult to predict from past metric patterns as anomalies. A deep autoencoder calculates reconstruction error for 30-minute windows, and statistical process control (SPC) signals a window when its error falls outside the control limits. Batch temporal normalization (BTN) is used to address non-stationary input data, and the method compares event patterns with anomalous statistics to suggest related events. In tests on other DBMSs, the author reports that BTN-equipped models detected disorder periods in ten cases, with the highest-scoring period matching the diagnosis in each case.
narrate.key_results: The autoencoder was trained on one month of data and the data was divided into 60% for training, 20% for validation, and 20% for testing. The model without BTN had the lowest reported test mean squared error (MSE), 0.3096, but the author reports that it did not detect anomaly periods effectively. The BTN model listed with test MSE 0.6912 was among the models reported; the author concluded that BTN helped the detector work with non-stationary multivariate series. In blind tests on ten disorder cases from other DBMSs, the detector produced multiple candidate periods, while the highest-error period matched the period identified by database administrators in all ten cases. The paper reports no run-length, false-alarm, or other numerical detection-performance measures.

key_equations.name: Window anomaly score
key_equations.explanation: The score is the average squared difference over a window of length T between observed values y and reconstructed values y-hat, for sample i and feature j at time t.

key_equations.name: Three-sigma control limits described for an average chart
key_equations.explanation: The upper and lower control limits are three standard deviations sigma above and below the center line; the paper describes this general average-chart rule but does not detail how limits for its reconstruction-error charts were estimated.

key_equations.name: Anomaly signal
key_equations.explanation: A window is treated as anomalous when its score lies outside the lower and upper control limits.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that it is difficult in practice to obtain labeled anomaly data for each DBMS. They note that, without such labels, numerical evaluation of detection results is difficult, and that additional training may be used after applying the pre-trained model.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers ten historical disorder cases and uses database administrators’ judgments rather than reported false-alarm rates, sensitivity, or run lengths, so operational detection performance is not quantified. The paper does not explain in detail how control limits are estimated for reconstruction scores or how their false-alarm behavior is maintained across different DBMSs. The training and test evidence is limited to selected DBMS statistics and examples; robustness to autocorrelation, non-normal reconstruction errors, and changing workloads is not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose additional training after transferring the pre-trained model and suggest recurrent or convolutional networks for representing sequential or local relationships. They also suggest using labeled anomaly data for numerical performance evaluation when such data can be obtained, and say that SPC decision rules, such as a two-sigma warning line, can be added.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could establish a transparent, validated method for calibrating control limits and measuring false alarms and detection delays under changing workload conditions. It could also test the method across broader operational DBMS data and develop a systematic way to validate or rank the suggested causal events after an anomaly signal.

narrate.summary: The paper develops cumulative sum (CUSUM) charts using signed sequential ranks (SSR) to monitor the location and dispersion of sequential observations from symmetric distributions. The location charts detect persistent shifts away from a specified median and can also respond to substantial asymmetry; a separate chart detects changes in dispersion. The chart updates a running score and signals when it crosses a control limit chosen to give a specified in-control average run length (ARL), without requiring a parametric distribution model or Phase I data. The authors find that these charts have distribution-free in-control behavior, and that the Van der Waerden version performs much like a normal CUSUM when data are normal, while the Wilcoxon version is useful for heavier-tailed data. An industrial example monitors differences between paired coal ash measurements from two laboratories.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with an in-control ARL of 500 and a change beginning at observation 50, Wilcoxon CUSUM ARLs in normal and t distributions with 3 degrees of freedom were generally close to normal-CUSUM approximations; for shifts greater than 0.25, the largest reported difference was 2 observations. For the Van der Waerden CUSUM at an in-control ARL of 500, shifts of 0.5 to 1.0 and change points at observations 50 or 100 gave ARL differences from the normal CUSUM of at most 4 observations when the shift met the stated target; differences were larger when the change began at the outset. In the coal data example, the Wilcoxon CUSUM signaled an increase in the mean at observation 235, with the change point estimated at observation 214; the reported means before and after that point were −0.027 and 0.595. The dispersion chart signaled at observation 238, but the authors judged this likely to be a response to the mean shift rather than a true dispersion change.

key_equations.name: Upper location-chart update and signal rule
key_equations.explanation: D_i is the upper chart value after observation i, ξ_i is its score, ζ is the reference value, and h is the upper control limit.

key_equations.name: Wilcoxon signed sequential rank score
key_equations.explanation: ξ_i is the score used by the Wilcoxon location chart, i is the observation index, s_i is the sign of the observation, and r_i⁺ is the sequential rank of its absolute value.

key_equations.name: Dispersion-chart score
key_equations.explanation: ξ_i is the score used by the dispersion chart, i is the observation index, and r_i⁺ is the sequential rank of the absolute observation.

key_equations.name: Post-change run length
key_equations.explanation: N is the first signal index, τ is the change point, and the expression is the expected time to signal after the change given that no signal occurred earlier.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the Wilcoxon location chart cannot detect shifts larger than 6.92 when the default reference value is used, because its score is bounded. Sequential ranks are not uniquely defined for observations arriving in unordered groups, so this method is not applicable to that data structure. The chart detects only substantial asymmetry efficiently, and the dispersion chart can eventually return to an in-control state after a dispersion change.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The distribution-free in-control guarantee relies on independent observations from a symmetric in-control distribution; the paper does not evaluate how serial dependence would affect its calibration. The simulations cover selected normal, Student t, and skew-normal distributions and shift scenarios, so they do not establish performance across a wider range of non-normal processes or against a broad set of competing charts. The operational example is one paired-measurement data set, and its chart signals required follow-up analysis to distinguish a mean change from a dispersion change.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate calibration and detection under autocorrelation, ties, and additional forms of non-normality, as well as compare these charts with a wider range of competing monitoring methods. Studies on more operational data sets could also develop systematic procedures for diagnosing whether a signal reflects a location, dispersion, or symmetry change.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors process measurements and controller settings to detect abnormal changes and help determine whether they come from a process disturbance or an attack. It uses multivariate statistical process control (MSPC) based on principal component analysis (PCA), with separate monitoring of score and residual statistics. An anomaly is signaled when three consecutive observations exceed the 99 percent control limit in either chart. Observation-based MEDA plots then show which variables contributed to the detected event. In simulated Tennessee-Eastman tests, monitoring both process and controller data made it possible to distinguish some attacks from a related disturbance, although denial-of-service diagnosis remained difficult.
narrate.key_results: The study ran each anomalous scenario 10 times and used 30 runs for calibration; each simulation lasted 72 hours unless the process shut down, and data were recorded 2,000 times per simulation hour. All tested disturbances and attacks were detected, using the rule that three consecutive observations must exceed the 99 percent control limit. Controller-level readings alone did not reliably distinguish a disturbance from a similar integrity attack, whereas comparing controller and process data allowed the authors to identify the origin in the tested cases. Detection was described as almost immediate for the disturbance and integrity-attack scenarios, but a denial-of-service attack took almost an hour; the paper does not give exact numerical average run lengths for each scenario.

key_equations.name: Principal component decomposition
key_equations.explanation: X is the mean-centered and auto-scaled data matrix, T_A is the score matrix, P_A is the loading matrix, E_A is the residual matrix, A is the number of retained components, and the superscript T denotes transpose.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that controller-level readings alone are insufficient to diagnose whether an anomaly is a disturbance or an attack. For denial-of-service events, detection is substantially slower and the diagnostic plots do not clearly identify the attacked variable.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses one simulated process and four tested anomaly scenarios, with 10 runs per scenario, so the findings may not generalize to other plants or attack patterns. The study does not compare its results against alternative monitoring charts, and it does not assess how estimation uncertainty from the 30 calibration runs affects false alarms or detection.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adding network-level information, such as packets, flows, and logs, to the process data. They expect these variables to improve diagnosis and shorten detection time, especially for network denial-of-service events.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on operational plant data and across different process types, disturbance patterns, and attack strategies. It could also investigate how to identify the source and extent of an event after a signal, and quantify performance under autocorrelation, non-normal data, and uncertainty in the estimated reference model.

narrate.summary: The paper monitors images of stochastic textured surfaces, such as woven fabric, for local defects that depart from normal spatial behavior. It learns the expected pixel values from neighboring pixels in representative in-control images and calculates residuals for new images. Local residual changes are summarized in moving windows using either an Anderson–Darling distribution comparison or a Box–Pierce covariance statistic; the largest local value in an image is compared with an upper control limit estimated from in-control images. If the limit is exceeded, a diagnostic image highlights locations with large local statistics. In simulated images and a textile example, the method detected a range of defects and generally performed better than the compared alternatives, with the Box–Pierce version often strongest.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation study, the reported average detection probabilities were based on 10 replicates and a per-image Type I error of 0.003. With the Box–Pierce statistic, detection probability was 0.955 for 5-by-5 defects with a window width of 5, at least 0.997 for 5-by-21 defects, and 1.000 for both 9-by-21 and 15-by-21 defects at all three tested window widths of 5, 15, and 25. In the textile example, the control limits were based on 94 in-control images, with one of those image statistics outside the limit; the Box–Pierce version signaled all six designed defect images at window widths of 15 and 25, and five of six at width 5. For comparison, the intensity-window method signaled none of the six textile defects, the modified wavelet method signaled one, and the local-variance window method signaled two; run-length results were not reported.

key_equations.name: Image monitoring statistic
key_equations.explanation: S_j is the monitoring statistic for image j, SMS_{j,i} is the spatial moving statistic at pixel i in image j, i indexes pixels, and M is the number of pixels considered.

key_equations.name: Empirical upper control limit
key_equations.explanation: UCL is the upper control limit, alpha is the desired per-image Type I error probability, S_j is the monitoring statistic for image j, and N is the number of in-control images used to estimate the limit.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that a larger moving window for the Box–Pierce statistic increases computation and leaves more boundary pixels unmonitored because full windows are required. They also note that window size affects detection, that defect size may not be known in advance, and that theoretical control-limit distributions are not available for their fitted models, so limits are estimated empirically from in-control images.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The reported false-alarm calibration and textile comparison rely on finite reference sets, including only 94 in-control textile images, so the estimated upper-tail limits may be uncertain, especially for very low false-alarm targets. Validation is also narrow: the simulation uses a particular Gaussian spatial autoregressive process and constructed defects, while the real-data demonstration uses designed textile defects rather than a broad set of naturally occurring production defects; performance under nonstationarity, changing spatial dependence, and other noise distributions is not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose accumulating image statistics over time with exponentially weighted or cumulative-sum methods when defects persist, combining charts with different window widths, and using different window widths near image boundaries. They also suggest alternative local statistics, more complex supervised-learning models, and methods to remove noise-related highlighted pixels from diagnostic images.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could quantify uncertainty in the fitted prediction model and empirical control limits, and test false-alarm control when reference images are limited or the surface departs from stationarity or the assumed neighborhood structure. Broader validation on independent production data and other surface types, together with evaluation of diagnostic accuracy and integration into inspection software, would clarify operational usefulness.
